74a19f23c8f72af9: Whenever you scan the headlines, a heart-breaking reality stares back: several Muslim-majority nations are trapped in devastating wars and armed conflicts. These crises range from full-scale international warfare to intense civil strife and localised insurgencies.

Tragically, from Iran, Iraq and Syria to Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, Somalia, Pakistan and Afghanistan, Muslims are often locked in conflict with other Muslims. This deep friction naturally prompts a difficult, uncomfortable question: can the Muslim world ever truly achieve unity?
On paper, the global ummah is bound by the most foundational of principles: belief in one God and the guidance of the Quran.
Yet, the reality on the ground is starkly fractured. It is easy for casual observers to look at this discord and assume that Islam itself is the root problem.

But if you pull back the curtain, it becomes clear that these conflicts are rarely about theology. Instead, they are driven by the exact same catalysts that spark wars anywhere else on earth: politics, money and human greed.
The truth is, most internal conflicts in the Muslim world are old-fashioned power struggles. Factions, regimes and politicians compete for control, territory and resources, plain and simple.

Consider the Sunni-Shia split. While it dates back to a seventh-century political disagreement over who should succeed Prophet Muhammad, these communities lived side-by-side in relative peace for centuries.
The divide only becomes weaponised today because authoritarian regimes and militant groups exploit it to manufacture an "us versus them" mentality.

Leaders routinely wrap their political ambitions in religious rhetoric because it remains a highly effective tool to manipulate the masses, justify violence and safeguard their power. This has been the norm in many failed Muslim states.

This dynamic plays out on a massive scale through regional chess games. Major powers like Saudi Arabia and Iran have long been locked in a geopolitical rivalry, turning vulnerable nations like Yemen and Syria into proxy battlegrounds.

Compounding the issue is that many modern borders in the region are fragile, artificially cutting across deep ethnic and tribal lines. When a central government collapses – as seen in Iraq or Libya – it creates a power vacuum that local armed groups immediately resort to violence to fill.
Coincidentally, many of these conflict zones are endowed with rich oil and gas reserves, making them highly attractive to foreign powers.

These natural resources are a double-edged sword: while they should guarantee prosperity, mismanagement leaves many states impoverished, even as the wealth draws predatory external interests. When warring domestic factions face defeat, they readily invite foreign intervention. Superpowers then step in under the guise of aid, though their true drivers are their own economic and strategic interests in the region.
Ultimately, a shared religious identity is not enough to sustain stability when states are hollowed out from within.

You cannot talk about unity without addressing daily survival. When high poverty, a lack of economic opportunity, systemic corruption and oppressive governance collide, they create a recipe for desperation. If citizens cannot build a decent life through peaceful or democratic means, sub-state conflicts and insurgencies become inevitable.

The path forward for the Muslim world is about repairing broken systems. Unity will only shift from a theological ideal to a political reality when leaders begin prioritising stable governance, economic fairness and basic human dignity over their political survival.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
1f88c4a4d3ae8faa: PETALING JAYA: Polis tidak sepatutnya mengambil alih tanggungjawab sekolah dalam menangani masalah ponteng, sebaliknya menumpukan perhatian kepada anasir luar yang mengambil kesempatan terhadap pelajar, kata pakar pendidikan.

Effendi@Ewan Matore daripada Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM) berkata, tugas mengesan kehadiran, menyiasat punca ketidakhadiran dan membimbing pelajar perlu kekal bawah tanggungjawab guru bimbingan dan kaunseling serta Jabatan Kebajikan Masyarakat (JKM).
Katanya, peranan polis lebih sesuai tertumpu kepada pendidikan berkaitan undang-undang, keselamatan jalan raya dan bahaya dadah, selain mengekang kegiatan pihak luar yang boleh memudaratkan pelajar.
“Antaranya termasuk sindiket dadah, premis tidak berlesen yang membenarkan pelajar berseragam berada di situ ketika waktu persekolahan serta kumpulan kongsi gelap yang cuba merekrut ahli baharu.

“Dari segi mandat, polis tidak mempunyai latihan pedagogi, kepakaran kerja sosial atau instrumen dasar untuk menangani punca asas keciciran pelajar, seperti kemiskinan keluarga, masalah pembelajaran atau krisis rumah tangga.
“Oleh itu, saya berpandangan penglibatan polis tidak sepatutnya menjurus kepada pemantauan tingkah laku peribadi atau pengumpulan profil keselamatan terhadap pelajar biasa,” katanya kepada FMT.

Beliau mengulas kenyataan Ketua Polis Kuala Lumpur, Fadil Marsus, pihaknya akan menjejak dan melakukan pemprofilan terhadap kira-kira 10% pelajar di ibu negara yang kerap ponteng serta tercicir daripada sistem persekolahan.
Fadil berkata, usaha itu bertujuan mengenal pasti punca keciciran dan membantu membawa pelajar terbabit kembali ke sekolah.

Sementara itu, Pengarah Pusat Kajian Pembangunan Ungku Aziz Universiti Malaya, Suhaiza Hanim Mohamad Zailani, berkata pemprofilan penting bagi mengenal pasti punca sebenar ketidakhadiran sebelum intervensi bersesuaian dilaksanakan.
Katanya, pelajar ponteng tidak seharusnya terus dianggap bakal pesalah, sebaliknya perlu dilihat sebagai individu yang mungkin memerlukan bantuan.
“Penglibatan polis boleh membantu jika terdapat ancaman keselamatan seperti kegiatan samseng, eksploitasi, penderaan atau jenayah yang menjejaskan kehidupan pelajar,” katanya.
Beliau berkata, bagi kes ponteng tanpa unsur ancaman sedemikian, intervensi perlu diterajui pihak pendidikan dengan kerjasama ibu bapa, kaunselor dan agensi kebajikan.
“Pemprofilan penting untuk memahami punca masalah supaya intervensi dapat disesuaikan dengan keperluan setiap pelajar, bukan menggunakan pendekatan sama untuk semua,” katanya.
Suhaiza berkata, pelajar mungkin ponteng akibat kesukaran kewangan, masalah pengangkutan, tanggungjawab menjaga ahli keluarga, tekanan untuk bekerja, buli atau ketinggalan dalam pembelajaran.
Katanya, membawa pelajar kembali ke sekolah tanpa menangani punca sebenar ketidakhadiran hanya menyelesaikan masalah buat sementara waktu.

Beliau turut mengingatkan, pendekatan yang terlalu menonjolkan penglibatan polis boleh menyebabkan pelajar berasa malu, takut atau dilabel sebagai pesalah, sekali gus mendorong mereka menjauhkan diri daripada sekolah.

“Justeru, proses pemprofilan perlu dilakukan secara berhemah dengan menjaga kerahsiaan pelajar serta memastikan maklumat yang dikumpulkan digunakan untuk merancang bantuan, bukannya menjadi rekod negatif yang membayangi masa depan mereka,” katanya.
461d2db7998800aa: KUALA KRAI: Nearly a decade ago, Azman Mustapha was eating lunch beside Sungai Koh when he noticed a few wild mahseer swimming in the clear water and tossed them some leftover rice.
At first, the fish darted away whenever he approached. Mahseer, known locally as ikan kelah, are notoriously sensitive to sound, movement and human presence.
But Azman kept returning and feeding them at roughly the same time each day. Over time, the fish began to associate him with food.

“That spontaneous act slowly became a daily routine. Day by day, more fish gathered here,” the 53-year-old told Bernama. “Now I feed them three to four times a day to encourage them to remain in this stretch of the river.”

Today, Azman estimates that hundreds of thousands of fish, including wild green mahseer, inhabit the stretch of river near Batu Mengkebang. The fish have grown more accustomed to human presence, and visitors can watch them gather in large numbers at feeding time.

“The greatest satisfaction is seeing visitors arrive and the fish no longer swim away,” he said, pointing out that in the early days, even the sound of footsteps along the riverbank could send them disappearing into deeper water.
“Getting wild mahseer used to people is not easy because they are extremely sensitive. It took me almost nine years to reach this stage," he added.

When feeding begins, the calm river can quickly fill with movement as the fish converge near the surface. For visitors, the sight of so many normally elusive mahseer in one place has become the main draw.
“When I see people’s excitement as the fish appear, I know every bit of effort has been worth it,” Azman said.
In 2023, he established FMC Kelah Eco Park beside the river, turning nearly 3km of Sungai Koh into a conservation-focused attraction.
“It’s an ecotourism destination built around protecting, rather than exploiting, the river’s natural ecosystem,” he noted.

That distinction matters because mahseer are highly prized as food fish. Farmed specimens can fetch hundreds of ringgit per kilogramme, but Azman said the wild fish in Sungai Koh are left undisturbed.

He has instead set up separate breeding ponds using broodstock obtained from external suppliers, allowing him to learn more about the species while meeting market demand without harvesting the river population.
For Azman, the value of the wild fish lies in the health of the river that sustains them.

Mahseer need clean, oxygen-rich water to thrive. Protecting the surrounding forest is therefore just as important, as unchecked development could cause erosion, degrade water quality and damage the ecosystem.
More than a fish sanctuary
The project has also begun drawing attention for its potential to support the surrounding community through nature-based tourism.
Universiti Malaysia Kelantan’s Institute for Poverty Research and Management has identified the park as an example of how conservation can be linked with rural development.
Its director, Ahmad Fahme Ali, said the river’s healthy mahseer population points to the importance of protecting natural habitats before trying to build tourism around them.

“We can clearly see that the mahseer’s natural habitat there remains intact and that its population continues to grow,” he said. “This shows the river ecosystem in that area has been well protected and carefully preserved.”

Senior lecturer Nur Ida Fatihah Che Shalifullizam added that nature-based tourism can create opportunities beyond the attraction itself, from food and accommodation to transport, recreation and small businesses.

For Azman, however, further growth comes with a condition. Better roads, electricity and visitor facilities may help the park develop, but he does not want expansion to damage the river that made it possible.
“If this river is damaged, the fish will disappear,” he stressed. “And when the fish are gone, everything we’ve built over the past decade will disappear with them.”

a423556ffaa01156: MELBOURNE: Australian mushroom murderer Erin Patterson lost a bid to overturn her convictions and had a harsher sentence imposed on Friday, failing to prove she was wrongfully jailed for killing three people with a poisoned lunch.
Patterson was found guilty last year of murdering her husband's parents and elderly aunt, deliberately lacing their beef Wellington meal with highly toxic death cap mushrooms.
The 52-year-old maintained her triple murder convictions were a "miscarriage of justice", urging the Court of Appeal in Victoria state to either set her free or have the case heard again.
The court found the killings were "carefully planned and deliberate", and there were insufficient grounds to try the case again.
"This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated," judge Stephen McLeish said.
"It stands to be denounced in the strongest terms."
Patterson has also been convicted of the attempted murder of her husband's uncle, a small-town local pastor who survived after weeks in hospital.
The court not only threw out Patterson's appeal, it also found that her original jail sentence did not match the gravity of her crimes.
Patterson was initially eligible to apply for release after 33 years.
The court ruled that she should not be eligible for parole, meaning Patterson is likely to die in prison.
Patterson did not front the trial in person, instead watching proceedings via video link from a maximum security prison on the outskirts of Melbourne.
Her lawyers had alleged a litany of irregularities in the trial, including an "oppressive" cross-examination and unfair decisions on the admission of evidence.
'Manifestly inadequate'
Prosecutors argued that the non-parole period of 33 years imposed by the judge was "manifestly inadequate".
They said the judge erred in finding there was a substantial chance Patterson would be held in solitary confinement for years to come, and this "infected" his decision on parole.
Patterson's trial last year drew podcasters, film crews and true crime fans to a courthouse in the rural town of Morwell, a sedate hamlet in Victoria better known for its prize-winning roses.
Audiences from New York to New Delhi followed every twist of what many now simply call the "mushroom murders".
The motive of the killings remains a mystery.

A 12-person jury found Patterson guilty in July last year of murdering her husband Simon's parents, Don and Gail Patterson, as well as his aunt, Heather Wilkinson, at her home in the Victorian farming village of Leongatha.
She was also found guilty of attempting to murder Heather's husband Ian, a pastor who fell gravely ill but eventually recovered.

ccbf2f56503f85ee: It seems like another season, but it was early this month when Anfield was meant to be the bear pit that would maul and then spit out the bad boys of Manchester City.

It was the first game after their guilty verdict and we all know how it went. Forgotten is that Liverpool gave City as good as they got before two harsh yellow cards to Ryan Gravenberch turned it all around.The bear was declawed and Liverpool’s 10 men couldn’t live with City, who ran out comfortable 3-0 winners.

That the Reds matched them for an hour didn’t fit the narrative of City defiance. Owners fiercely maintaining their innocence, players with a siege mentality, fans with inflatable bananas… all wallowing in victimhood.
They managed to win their first seven games, but then United stole their thunder with yet another crisis of their own.
After this Mancunian monopoly of headlines, it is time to go back to Liverpool, not least because Arsenal are the next visitors.
Smarting from their loss to Fleetwood, the champions will be a good test of where Liverpool are in the pecking order right now.
For there is the unmistakable whiff of meaningful momentum about them.
The roar that greeted Wesley Fofana’s penalty miss in midweek was more like the Kop we knew.
It was only a shoot-out, only the League Cup, and there were extra decibels for Chelsea, but it resonated.
Not ‘off the Richter’ like the Kop’s deafening best, but it saluted another win, their fifth in a row since the loss to City.
Two were in the Champions League (against Villarreal and LASK) that helped them to third place in the table with a 100% record.
Two in the EPL against hard-to-beat Brentford and Brighton, and now this to reach the last eight of the Carabao Cup.
And there was the added satisfaction of beating two former employees.
Xabi Alonso, who had been warmly welcomed as Bayer Leverkusen boss, was made aware what a cardinal sin it is to join Chelsea, at least in the eyes of the Kop.
But it was former skipper Jordan Henderson, who came in for most of the stick.
“Hendo’s” sterling service in Jurgen Klopp’s greatest sides was brusquely erased from memory by the sight of him in Chelsea blue.
Besides being loftily placed in three competitions, there are many reasons for optimism around the Reds right now.
The rebuild is not yet finished, but there has been unexpected progress.
Top of the list is that the stalled £400m strike force is firing.
Even the most recent – and expensive – addition, Bradley Barcola, is showing why the Reds paid PSG £125m for him after a sluggish start.
His pace is electric and although he’s very different to Mo Salah, his versatility is giving the attack more flexibility.
But the biggest improvement has come in the form of Alexander Isak, who had such a horrendous start to his Anfield career.
The Swede is now looking more like the player they broke the club record for. Cody Gakpo is also more of a force than last season, having brought his international form to the EPL.
This leaves Florian Wirtz. To say that Iraola is getting a tune out of the £116m man may still require a hearing aid.
He’s had better moments but is still way short of the little maestro they thought they were getting.
Then there’s the waspish Munoz buzzing across the entire attack, and it’s no wonder with assets like these, the Reds are mostly on the front foot.
Coupled with the ‘coming out’ of Rio Ngumoha ahead of schedule, and the teenager’s ability to flourish on both wings, too, manager Andoni Iraola has the sort of headache he doesn’t mind.

He’s been rewarded for his faith in youth by the emergence of Trey Nyoni too, and in a position where the club offered £100m fees in vain a couple of seasons ago. Ngumoha and Nyoni, a magical pair and money-savers too.
Let’s not forget Hugo Ekitike, who hopes to return from his ruptured Achilles by the end of the year.
The good news for Liverpool is that the Frenchman, who was by far the best signing of the previous transfer window, is already back working on the ball.
With that type of injury, there’s no guarantee he’ll be as lightning-fast as he once was, but his recovery is on course.
If he does return to his old form, Liverpool could boast the best attack in the business.
If attack is Liverpool’s forte, there’s encouragement all over the park. Ronald Araujo has been a masterly piece of business and gone from stopgap to cult hero playing out of position.
Whatever Barcelona want for the Uruguayan must be paid, according to his adoring fans.
Jeremy Jacquet has also made a brilliant start and looks to be Virgil van Dijk’s successor already.
And Giorgio Mamardashvili may have finally won the sceptics over with his showing against Chelsea.
The prevailing view is that Iraola has done well to fit them into the jigsaw so quickly and return Liverpool to something more like the heavy metal style of Klopp.
A slow starter – he went 10 games at Bournemouth before claiming his first win – and with the huge step up in size of club, it was felt he might need a few months to get it right.
But to have the team where they are before the end of October suggests he could become a major managerial figure.
Having come out on top – albeit narrowly – over one of his former Basque colleagues in Alonso, he now faces another in Mikel Arteta.
It’s too soon to talk of a title challenge, but if he can find a way to beat the depth of the Gunners, it won’t mean Liverpool are back, but that they are coming back.
That’s pretty good given the upheaval the club has been through.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

9370750c9f4c323d: Multiple vulnerabilities in five popular AI developer tools could allow attackers to execute code on a host machine, read and steal files, or spoof browser address bars. Researchers say flaws in OpenAI's Codex and Microsoft's VS Code remain unpatched, potentially putting developers who use affected configurations at risk.

AI security startup Forever Security discovered vulnerabilities in Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Anthropic's Claude Desktop, VS Code, and Codex, and disclosed four of the flaws to the affected vendors. GitHub independently fixed the Copilot vulnerability without receiving a report from Forever Security. All five share a common security weakness: embedded browsers granted capabilities beyond those available to conventional browsers.

Each tool “enriched its embedded browser beyond what a normal browser allows, and those enrichments undermined the traditional threat model - as agent input, as the authority on a tab’s own address, or as reach onto the host,” Forever researcher Gal Weizman wrote in a Thursday report.

Forever dubbed this class of vulnerability “Embrace,” short for EMbedded BRowser, and said the flaws led to code execution in Cursor, data theft in Claude Desktop, Codex, and VS Code, and address bar spoofing in GitHub Copilot.
Here’s what each of these looks like, starting with Cursor.
Cursor: arbitrary code execution
Typical web pages can’t run commands on the host computer because a web page’s JavaScript cannot talk to local apps.

Cursor’s integrated browser, however, allows a page to call the agent’s composer. The agent reads this as instructions and follows them, but the instructions remain hidden from human users. This opens the coding agent up to prompt injection attacks that could allow an attacker to execute commands on the host machine.

The researchers disclosed the vulnerability to Cursor on September 10, and the vendor silently patched the flaw on October 1. According to Forever, Cursor did not publish a security advisory about the issue or respond to the researchers' disclosure.
Cursor also did not reply to The Register’s request for comment.
GitHub Copilot: address bar spoofing
Under normal browser operations, a webpage cannot change the content of the address bar.

“Copilot’s browser preview works differently,” Weizman wrote. “Some pages change their address without loading a new page, and the app cannot always see that. So Copilot let the page tell the app its own address.”

The app checked only whether the text looked like a web address, starting with http, https or file, but it didn’t check where the tab really pointed to. This can be abused to trick the embedded browser into displaying a spoofed URL - such as github.com/login - in the address bar, while loading a fraudulent website - like a phishing page - underneath.

The researchers found the address-bar spoofing flaw in GitHub Copilot 1.1.27 on September 26. GitHub independently fixed the flaw in a later Copilot build (1.1.29) on October 13 without receiving a vulnerability report from Forever.
We reached out to GitHub and did not receive a response.
Claude Desktop, Codex, and VS Code: arbitrary file read
All three of these vendors’ coding assistants allow local HTML files opened in the built-in browser to escape its boundaries and access other files.

Both Claude Desktop and VS Code allow local pages access to their respective project folders, but the researchers found that these restrictions did not apply to web workers – a browser feature that allows JavaScript to run in a background thread, separate from the page's main thread.
This means a local page can start a worker, and the worker can bypass restrictions to reach any file on the machine.
Codex, however, didn’t have this same restriction, meaning a local page could read any file directly without a worker.

Weizman said his team disclosed the issue to Anthropic on July 23, and the AI vendor declined the Claude Desktop bug report as invalid for a “workspace trust” gated security boundary. A day later, however, Noma Security reported the same flaw, according to Weizman, and Anthropic accepted the report as valid.
Anthropic did not respond to The Register’s questions about either bug report or Forever’s timeline of events.

Forever disclosed the Codex bug to OpenAI on July 27 and didn’t get a response. The security team says it’s still unpatched. OpenAI did not respond to our inquiries, including if it planned to fix the flaw.

On September 10, Forever disclosed the VS Code vulnerability to Microsoft and says the vendor also labeled it as an invalid workspace trust gated security boundary issue. The researchers claim it remains unpatched. Microsoft did not respond to our request for comment.®

ff28614e0b2a21a4: ‘No independent body regularly monitored developments in prisons and communicat’d this information to the public using data.
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot from Prison Agenda‘s Substack page, used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

In Turkey, a team of two journalists and human rights activists launched a digital publication, Prison Agenda, to report on what is happening inside the country’s prisons and prison system, information that is often hidden from the Turkish public and the world.

As the Nordic Monitor noted in 2025, Turkey’s prison population has reached an unprecedented level. Citing figures from the Directorate General of Prisons and Houses of Detention, the website states that as of September 1, 2025, Turkish prisons hold 419,194 individuals. This includes 356,710 convicted prisoners and 62,484 people in pretrial detention. The figure exceeds the official capacity of 295,000 and places immense strain on the country’s penal system.

Le Monde also wrote in 2026 that a commissioned report on prison conditions among Council of Europe member states showed that France and Turkey each had 131 inmates for every 100 places, making them the two most overcrowded prison systems.

For the relatives of people in prison, as well as for national and international human rights organizations and agencies, the information provided by the Prison Agenda publication can be vital. A similar organization — Russia Behind Bars — used to work in Russia. While it did not function exclusively as a publication, it received letters from prisoners and their relatives, published news about torture or other human rights violations, and reported how the prison population had been drafted, in the hundreds of thousands, to fight Russia’s war with Ukraine. Unfortunately, it had to shut down its work within Russia because of the regime’s prosecution, but it continues to inform from abroad.

Civil society organizations, such as the publication about Prisons and Prisoners, are vital to the country and the world; they need to continue their important work within one of the most opaque systems in the world.
Global Voices interviewed one of Prison Agenda’s founder, Ahmet Kavruk, by email.
GV: Please tell us about your organization, and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project?

Ahmet Kavruk (AK): Prison Agenda is a digital publication that covers data on Turkey’s prisons, legislative changes relating to prisons, and human rights violations within them. It is guided by an independent, rights-focused approach to journalism.

We launched in January 2026. Our aim is to make the often complicated and scattered information about prisons more accessible to the public by presenting it in a clear and understandable way, and to highlight the human stories behind the statistics.

Shortly after launching in January, we reached a crossroads. We could either continue as a passion project, publishing solely in Turkish, which would be easier to sustain, but would not fulfil our potential, or evolve into a publishing model that would require more intensive work, but enable us to reach a wider audience.

It was precisely at this decision-making stage that we came across the Digital Spark call for proposals. It was one of the few support programmes capable of creating space for initiatives working in specific and often overlooked fields, such as prisons. We, therefore, drew up a plan and, should we be accepted into Digital Sparks, began to focus on the question, ‘How can we grow the Prison Agenda?’

We were particularly impressed by Digital Spark’s approach, which focuses on amplifying the voices of marginalized groups and strengthening civic participation. The fact that the project’s core objectives aligned so closely with our own area of work was a decisive factor in our decision to join the programme.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

AK: We are currently a team of two. We are both individuals with over 10 years’ experience working and producing within the prison sector in various capacities. We were aware of the growing problems in Turkey’s prisons. Through our voluntary work, professional lives and social networks, we have been trying to raise awareness of these issues.

However, our work in this field revealed not only these problems, but also a significant shortcoming. No independent body regularly monitored developments in prisons and communicated this information to the public using data. The data was scattered, technical and often difficult to access. Meanwhile, media interest tended to intensify only when there was new legislation or a high-profile incident.

Drawing on our background in journalism and our experience in human rights monitoring, we believed we could address this gap. We, therefore, launched Prison Agenda, aiming to present existing information to the public in a clear, accessible, rights-focused manner.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

AK: The most significant change for us during this project was launching our bilingual publications. By switching to English, we were able to reach beyond our existing Turkish audience and connect with a very different group of readers. The feedback from this new audience further strengthened our belief in the project’s potential.

While we initially had just one e-newsletter, we diversified our publications over time, increasing our regular e-newsletters to three. Today, Prison Agenda has evolved from a publication that shares news into a comprehensive digital media organisation that produces investigative reports, data analyses, data visualisations, thematic content, and opinion pieces.

This transformation aligns with our initial project goals of bilingual publishing and data-driven content production. In the first six months, our Turkish and English newsletters reached a total of 435 subscribers.
AK: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

AK: While our Turkish-language publications are mainly followed by the press, legislators and civil society, we have noticed that our English-language publications are attracting the attention of diplomatic missions from various countries and international-level bureaucrats. This was a significant development for us as it created an opportunity to raise awareness of prison issues in Turkey within a wider international network.

Throughout the project, we received collaboration proposals from different organisations and groups. The number of news articles citing our data and content increased, raising Prison Agenda's profile. Additionally, we started providing advice on data, sources and content to journalists reporting on prisons.

This has ensured that the information we produce is not limited to our own readers, but is made available within a wider ecosystem. We hope the network of readers and stakeholders established by Prison Agenda will help to raise awareness of prisoners’ rights and the need for humane prison conditions. The project’s aim was, indeed, to strengthen civil oversight and accountability by making information more accessible.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

AK: Prisons are, by their very nature, a rather closed field of work, with limited overlap with many other areas of rights. For this reason, we are not always able to collaborate with other civil society organisations.

One of the most significant opportunities that Digital Sparks has created for us is the chance to share a space with different civil society organisations and learn about their work first-hand. We have met groups working on issues outside our own field, developing different methods, and those who are just starting out. These encounters have enabled us to share knowledge and view our own work from an outside perspective.

One of the most significant realisations for us during this process was that civil society is much larger and broader than we had previously realised. Because Prison Agenda works in a very specific field, we realised that we were sometimes limited to our immediate circle. However, Digital Sparks showed us that this field is much broader and that there are far more areas where different struggles can intersect.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

AK: Digital Spark was the first support we received. Although we had previously been involved in various projects as part of a team, this was the first time we had been part of a project where the full responsibility rested directly with us. For this reason, it was also a new learning experience for us.

This was actually the part that challenged us the most. We learnt that a project is not limited to simply producing content and activities; it also requires managing its budget, administrative processes, reporting and responsibilities.

One of the most tangible things we learnt during this process was financial reporting. While our previous experience in this area was limited, carrying out the reporting processes required by the project provided us with valuable practical experience.

Consequently, Digital Sparks was not merely a project through which we developed Prison Agenda’s publishing capacity; it was also a significant experience in a small team transforming into a structure capable of standing on its own two feet, managing its responsibilities, and planning for the future.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

AK: Although we’re a very new organisation, we’re just as eager and enthusiastic. We have many options before us that could take us in different directions, as well as ideas that we’re keen to develop.

For example, we’re currently refining a public prison database project, and we’re also preparing to run a training course on prison journalism in the new year. We have a wide variety of datasets at our disposal that we want to make accessible to a wider audience. In the long term, we also plan to increase the number of areas we cover and deepen the content we produce in these fields.

We believe that we have not yet reached our natural limits. The digital capacity we have developed through Digital Sparks has opened up significant scope for us to expand these limits. In the near future, we intend to use the knowledge and experience we have gained to prioritise our readers, understand their requirements, and integrate their feedback into our editorial strategy.

Our aim is to transform the Prison Agenda into a structure that produces more content and enables more people to access information on prisons, bringing together different stakeholders in the process.
Written by Daria Dergacheva

736806315d48a460: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 30 — Pet owners could soon claim tax relief on adoption, vaccination and sterilisation expenses under a proposal announced in Budget 2027.
The move is aimed at helping pet owners offset some of the costs associated with caring for animals, from routine vaccinations to one-off expenses such as adoption and sterilisation.
Pet ownership costs have gradually risen over the years and, for some households, have become a growing part of monthly spending.
Instead of creating a separate allowance, the proposed relief would fall under the existing RM2,500 lifestyle tax relief limit.
The actual tax savings would depend on eligible spending, the taxpayer's applicable income tax rate and how much of the relief limit remains unused.
What pet owners are paying
Published fees from animal welfare organisations and veterinary providers offer an indication of what pet owners might pay.
Costs vary according to the animal, type of vaccine, size, sex and services included.
All figures are illustrative examples from selected published price lists, not standard rates or national averages.
Actual fees may vary by provider, location, animal and services required.
Adoption fees may include vaccination and sterilisation, so pet owners should avoid counting included services again as separate expenses.
As a pet owner, Diyana Malek said that unless her cat falls sick, she hardly spends anything on it apart from food and supplements.
“Even tick or flea medication could cost hundreds, depending on the size of the cat or dog. The prices of this medication vary.
“I send my cat to the veterinary clinic for showers. The price for that follows the weight of the cat and that starts from RM80.
“So this tax relief helps, it takes off a reasonable load,” Diyana said when contacted by Malay Mail.
The price of an average tick/flea medication ranges from RM60 to RM92, depending on the brand.
How much could pet owners save?
Using published prices as an illustration, a household with two cats and one dog could incur the following costs for vaccination and sterilisation.
If the full RM570 qualified for tax relief, the potential tax savings would depend on the taxpayer’s applicable marginal tax rate:
11 per cent = RM62.70
18 per cent = RM102.60

These are illustrative estimates, not guaranteed savings. The actual benefit would depend on the taxpayer’s chargeable income, applicable tax rate, eligible expenses and how much of the RM2,500 lifestyle relief limit remains unused.
The calculation also assumes the household pays the listed fees separately.
It does not include adoption costs or account for any vaccination or sterilisation services already covered by an adoption fee.
What pet owners should know
The proposed relief would be included within the existing RM2,500 lifestyle tax relief limit, which also covers other eligible expenses.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The proposed relief would be included within the existing RM2,500 lifestyle tax relief limit, which also covers other eligible expenses. — Picture by Choo Choy May
It would not give pet owners an additional RM2,500 allowance solely for animal care.
This means taxpayers who have already used the full limit may not receive additional relief from their pet-related expenses.
The proposal covers eligible vaccination and sterilisation services provided by registered veterinary services, as well as the cost of adopting a rescued pet from a registered animal shelter.
Since the detailed eligibility conditions and documentation requirements have yet to be announced, pet owners should check their claims against the final rules before submitting them.
a25c846fcd0ef092: SAN LUIS (Arizona), Oct 30 — Between the hundreds of migrants arriving every day to seek asylum, chases of those fleeing, and the encounters with drug traffickers, Jason Mercado was overwhelmed during his time working for the US Border Patrol under Joe Biden.
“It’s peaceful now,” the retired agent says as he stands in front of the enormous wall that separates the United States from Mexico, near the town of San Luis, Arizona.
On the eve of the midterm elections, this arid region in the Southwest serves as proof that Donald Trump kept his central campaign promise: to restore order at the border.
In the sector around San Luis, the Border Patrol now apprehends fewer than 10 people per day — a sharp decline from the up to 2,000 per day under the last administration.
This drop, which began during the final months of the Biden presidency, accelerated under the Republican billionaire’s aggressive anti-immigration offensive.

Now filing an asylum claim at the border has become extremely difficult; migrants apprehended near the wall are almost never released while awaiting a hearing; and high-profile, forceful operations targeting undocumented immigrants across the United States have served as a deterrent.
Mercado’s former colleagues tell him that during their patrols, things are “very quiet.”
“One or two of them said the word ‘boring,’” says the 56-year-old, a Republican voter, with a smile.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A larger port of entry is under construction at the US-Mexico border in San Luis, Arizona October 19, 2026. In the sector around San Luis, the Border Patrol now apprehends fewer than 10 people per day — a sharp decline from the up to 2,000 per day under the last administration. — AFP pic
Relief
In the small town of San Luis, the sense of relief is palpable, even among Democrats, who sometimes struggled with the scope of the humanitarian crisis.

Churches and community organisations provided food and shelter for thousands of people in transit, while the hospital in Yuma, the county seat, was completely overwhelmed, and the federal government still owes it millions.
“Our tax dollars were going toward all of that,” says Georgina Escamilla, speaking in Spanish in her Mexican restaurant.
“They were giving money to people coming from other countries, while those who live here receive no help,” adds the 63-year-old, who leans to the left politically.
Yet, the return of calm masks a new sense of unease among the residents of this agricultural region — one of the country’s primary producers of lettuce and other vegetables.
“With Trump, we’ve shot ourselves in the foot,” complains Ricardo Vasquez.
The 58-year-old farmworker is frustrated that he now has to pay more than 20 per cent more for diesel, a cost he attributes to the conflict in Iran initiated by the president.
“The country wasn’t doing so badly before he arrived, and now, with fuel prices, it feels like we’re being slapped in the face, because everything is going up,” he grumbles.

In his fields of lettuce and broccoli, Mike Pasquinelli no longer has to worry about the destruction caused by migrants fleeing the police — incidents that previously wiped out portions of his harvest.
However, the surge in the cost of diesel and fertilisers, driven by the conflict in the Middle East, is eating into his bottom line.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

After the irrigating a vegetable field, farm workers remove the irrigation system pipes, in Somerton, Arizona, on October, 18, 2026. In his fields of lettuce and broccoli, Mike Pasquinelli no longer has to worry about the destruction caused by migrants fleeing the police — incidents that previously wiped out portions of his harvest. — AFP pic
‘Uncertainty’
“We’re probably gonna have about a 20 per cent reduction in profits... compared to last year,” sighs the farmer, who serves as president of the Yuma Fresh Vegetables Association.
He has also had to contend with a drop in orders, stemming from tensions linked to the trade war with Canada, a major destination for his vegetable exports.
“There’s been a lot of uncertainty on the foreign market, especially with the tariffs and retaliation between countries,” he says.
“Most of the market has stabilised, but we’ve had some ups and downs.”
This instability has also taken a toll on the logistics sector, another key employer in the region.
In his refrigerated warehouses, located right up against the border wall — in an area through which dozens of trucks pass — Mario Jauregui is fed up with “always playing the guessing game.”
Tariffs, which have been repeatedly imposed and then lifted, have cut the volume of fruit his clients ship between Mexico and the United States by a fifth.
His industry is also facing setbacks because the Trump administration has stopped issuing commercial vehicle permits to certain foreign drivers.
“It’s become so uncertain... nowadays that when we wake up the first thing that we do is look at the news,” the conservative business owner grumbles.
“I don’t think that that’s a way to manage a country.”
At 66, he has always voted Republican.
But with the November 3 election approaching, he finds himself hoping that Trump’s Republican Party loses its congressional majority.
“I would much rather have a Democratic Congress and a Republican president,” he says with a sigh. “We need to learn our lesson.” — AFP
6d0c83d2b64fda06: So now “gomen” employees can’t use Waze, the popular navigation app. This is a truly funny-but-not-funny situation. Somebody must have invoked some scary natural security scenarios about the dangers this US-owned, Israeli-founded company poses to our nation.

Here’s why this isn’t trivial. A company I once worked in experienced a massive computer hack. Experts from overseas were brought in to investigate. Panic reigned at the top. What I remember most from the briefings by the experts was the experts saying that everyone in the industry has either been hacked, or has been hacked and didn’t know about it.
I felt rather naked knowing somebody somewhere has a lot of detailed info about me, even if the only juicy details were about at which street corners were the best char kuey teow stalls.

It turns out one of the easiest ways to hack a human target and steal information more critical than just the locations of char kuey teow stalls is to hack their co-workers, assistants, family, friends, or football buddies and not necessarily the targets themselves.

That’s not as exciting as what happens in a James Bond movie, but rather the more plodding and low-key style of a John le Carre novel. One way or another, though, with enough cunning and guile and resources, people can find out a lot of things that others would prefer left hidden.
Why they snoop

Digital surveillance has become a massive business as well as a national security tool – checking what, when, and where we went or bought or spoke, as well as where we browsed on the internet and what social media content we generated or consumed. Artificial Intelligence has made it all easier.

The purpose of all this snooping is often just to sell you stuff, but increasingly it’s also becoming a way to control people and societies and even conduct warfare - as in the case of Elon Musk personally throttling his Starlink and Starshield services to Ukraine, thus harming Ukraine’s war efforts. That was one of the reasons many European nations are building digital alternatives to what Musk and the US offer, a trend that’s only gaining speed.

They're not just looking for alternatives for the latest digital stuff, either. Many nations have begun cutting off links they have relied on for decades with nations they no longer deem reliable for software, data centres and cloud services, computer chips, critical scientific research etc.

The big powers, especially the US and China, have been manipulating each other and others for years. China, which is fast catching up with the West in digital capabilities, looks safer today by comparison, but certainly they’re playing this same game too.
The Malaysian way

After banning Waze, Malaysia took the obvious next step by recommending the use of a home-grown alternative called TuJu, an app apparently running off the same backbone as Waze, but hosting all the captured data in some secure local data centres.

I haven’t downloaded TuJu, or used it in any shape or form. I know the locations of the best char kuey teow stalls by heart and can get there come rain or shine or traffic jams or anything else, up to a haze API level of 200. I'm fine, thank you.

Of course, we’re going about this the typical time-honoured Malaysia-Boleh way. First the government declares a critical national objective – industrialisation, national security, safety, pandemic response, etc.—and then, lo and behold, there appears a ready-made Malaysian solution!

We’ve seen this all before. The secrecy behind such decisions is often at a high level. Don’t forget even a toll highway concession agreement between the government and private parties is considered a sensitive national secret. Malaysia Boleh often actually means Malaysia Tak Boleh for the rest of us.

What little I know about TuJu doesn’t give me much confidence. The names associated with it seems to be the usual cast of characters of door openers to lucrative government contracts and not quite young genius alumni of the world’s top research universities or tech corporations or research institutions.
The other way

When it comes to high-tech, especially digital ones, I’m sceptical of people of my age and generation. We’re often the generation that calls AI “A-One”, as a famous episode involving a US cabinet member – handling education of all things! – hilariously reveals.

I wouldn’t even trust myself, even if I’m actually AI personified! The only good thing I can design and develop would be maps on napkins about the aforementioned char kuey teow locations which are, if I’m honest, not that great, after all.

But I’ve thought about making my own digital contributions during these critical times because it seems any old fogey can do it. I plan to release TuDia, an app that points out where you need to go; TangTu and TangNi to tell you when you’ve arrived here or there, and TuPun and TuLah to argue or commiserate with you when you’re lost.

And why not? The needs are real and urgent. All I’m asking for is complete access to all Malaysians’ personal data with a promise not to sell it to Elon Musk or Israel under a 50-year exclusive agreement that’ll be classified as a national secret forever.
Ah, silly dreams. I think all that’ll happen to me is, as Penangites like to say, that I’ll Pi Mai Pi Mai Tang Tu Jugak.
Which may work out as the name of another app that describes life in Malaysia Bolehland.

4e776a100c80e4cc: Sebenarnya saya malas nak tulis pasal bendera terbalik lagi sebab dah banyak kali tulis. Kumpulan ini dipercayai rakyat Malaysia dari Sabah dan Sarawak yang menggelarkan diri mereka Sabah dan Sarawak Keluar Malaysia (SSKM). Perbuatan ini saya anggap ‘agak berat’ dan perlu suatu komentar terhadapnya dengan cara baik dan beradab daripada bidasan dan cemuhan media sosial yang tidak terkawal.

Pertama sekali saya ingin mengucapkan terima kasih kepada menteri di Jabatan Perdana Menteri dari Sabah, Mustapha Sakmud. Beliau memberi teguran dan nasihat yang beradab dan bernas maka saya harap oang di Australia itu dengar baik-baik. Jangan terlajak kata nanti masa depan binasa. Sekarang mungkin gagah di Australia tetapi sepandai tupai melompat silap hari bulan kena balik negara sendiri semula. Siapa tahu nasib kita kecuali tuhan. Jadi, kalau kita dah ada rumah dan keluarga di sesuatu corner of the world, jangan cepat-cepat perlekeh, nanti kita juga yang terpaksa mencarinya di akhir hayat.

Isu bendera yang lalu bagi saya cukup jelas semuanya tidak disengajakan. Dari Editor Sin Chew kepada Kementerian Pendidikan, kesilapan Umno dan PAS Terengganu dan juga ‘Apek Tua’ di Pulau Pinang semuanya not on purpose. Ada yang tersilap dan ada yang cuai terlepas pandang sebab tidak pergi semak kerja suruhan kita sendiri. Saya telah mencadangkan supaya kita semua maaf-maafkan dan let it go tetapi jangan ulang lagi. Walaupun ada juga orang Umno yang suka mendabik dada sebagai paling patriotik mencemuh, menghina dan mengugut pihak yang tersilap pasang bendera, saya selalu menasihatkan individu tersebut supaya bertenang dan jangan cuba cari modal politik seperti ini.

Namun demikian, orang itu mendapat banyak political mileage dengan sandiwaranya. Saya tidak nampak pula beliau bising pasal bendera terbalik yang disengajakan orang Sabah dan Sarawak di Australia. Mungkin sebab Sabah dan Sarawak bakal sebagai king makers dalam PRU16. Kalau Onn Hafiz Ghazi gunakan istilah selective prosecution kini kita lihat ada parti yang buat selective criticism dalam isu bendera terbalik dengan sengaja.

Kembali kita kepada orang Sabah dan Sarawak di Australia ini, bagaimana kita nak nasihatkan mereka selain daripada apa yang dikatakan menteri di Jabatan Perdana Menteri itu? Biar saya guna analogi keluarga saya sebagai nasihat dan renungan untuk hidup berkeluarga. Sabah, Sarawak dan Semenanjung adalah sebuah keluarga dari aspek politik kenegaraan. Sabah dan Sarawak telah bersama Semenanjung Tanah Melayu selama 63 tahun. Umur saya sekarang 64 tahun. Saya mempunyai seorang isteri, lima orang anak, tiga orang menantu dan empat orang cucu. Ada tiga perkara penting dalam kita hidup berkeluarga.

Pertama, jangan sekali-kali guna perkataan cerai, nyah atau get out of the family. Kalau sebolehnya jangan langsung terkeluar kata-kata itu sehingga kita menghembus nafas terakhir di dunia ini. Walau apa perit sekali pun we do not say those words. Kata pepatah Melayu air yang dicincang tidak akan putus. Wise Malays. Melayu lama memang cerdik, tetapi Melayu baharu nampak terlalu gopoh-gapah. Tuhan telah menyatukan saya dan isteri. Selepas itu tuhan kurniakan kami tiga anak perempuan dan dua anak lelaki. Akhir sekali tuhan kurniakan kami semua empat orang cucu daripada perkahwinan anak-anak perempuan kami. Anak lelaki dua orang masih eligible kalau ada yang nak apply. Memang semua perkahwinan antara dua orang manusia berbeza akan ada isu, krisis dan macam-macam cabaran. Looking back semua cabaran itu 99% adalah dari diri kita sendiri dan bukan pun pasal orang lain buat. Sungguh. Blaming others for out own shortcoming is the easiest thing in the world. Jadi, kena refleksi dalaman dulu sebelum mengata salah orang ini dan orang itu. Apabila saya sakit jantung, sakit darah perut dan melalui severe panic disorder, isteri saya was by my side every time. Ada ketika yang kita tak berduit hingga kena pinjam abang sendiri atau minta anak buat loan. Itu semua lumrah hidup. We need family. Siapa lagi yang nak tolong.

Kedua, saya membina rumah di Kajang sebagai a refuge untuk semua anak saya. Saya dah siapkan konsep lima ‘studio apartmen’ yang lengkap dengan tandas, dapur, living room dan tempat tidur selesa serta aircond setiap bilik. Saya kata kalau kamu bergaduh dengan suami atau isteri you can come back and cool off di Kajang. Saya tahu berdasarkan pengalaman saya dan isteri, you cannot avoid conflicts jadi kita kena manage ia dengan menyediakan alternative refuge dan juga tempat untuk mereka mengadu. Saya dan isteri selalu mendengar keluhan anak-anak perempuan tentang suami mereka dan selalu kami mengajukan kesabaran dan pengalaman kami sendiri. Jangan cepat kita bercerai-berai atau mengadu domba sama ada dalam keluarga manusia atau keluarga negara. We can always manage whatever conflict kalau kita tidak burn the bridge dengan sesiapa.

Ketiga adalah tempat kami sediakan untuk cucu. Cucu adalah kurniaan tuhan yang amat penting bagi kehidupan kami semua. Saya sebagai ‘atuk’ dan isteri sebagai ‘nenek’ menjadikan rumah di Kajang sebagai resort bila hujung minggu dan di hari-hari cuti sekolah panjang di mana papa dan mama dua-dua bekerja di pejabat masing-masing. Saya tidak suka cucu saya ditinggalkan bertiga tanpa penyeliaan orang dewasa. Ada juga keadaan di mana bila krisis keluarga berlaku, mereka boleh menetap secara indefinitely di Kajang sehingga krisis berlalu. Seperti juga sesebuah negara, kalau kita mempunyai krisis di tempat tinggal di luar negara maka ke Malaysia jugalah kita pulang. Maka itu jangan senang-senang menolak negara atau menyisihkannya hanya kerana satu dua isu yang boleh diselesaikan dengan masa dan hikmah.

Sebagai mesej politik, kita semua ada negara dan ada keluarga dalam negara itu. Kita semua rakyat Malaysia di Semenanjung, Sabah dan Sarawak. Ia suatu gagasan penting bagi kita semua. Memang akan sentiasa ada konflik atau isu kaum, agama, politik dan sebeban lagi tetapi jika kita teguh dalam satu famili dan ada tempat untuk berlabuh maka kedua-duanya adalah important asset bagi kita. Menterbalikkan dan mencarik bendera negara dengan sengaja adalah suatu perkara yang cukup berat bagi saya. Ia sama dengan beberapa mahasiswa yang bakar gambar perdana menteri yang saban hari bekerja kuat. Itu mungkin budaya Barat atau Australia. Mungkin kumpulan tersebut hendak bakar, carik atau menterbalikkan bendera Australia pula di bawah freedom of expression di lain hari pula? Apa makna loyalty to family dan nation kalau begitu. Apa makna perbincangan dan bertolak ansur dalam hubungan antara manusia kalau jambatan dibakar terlebih dulu? Jambatan yang runtuh tidak boleh memanfaatkan sesiapa yang mungkin ada solusi baharu di masa hadapan.
Renung-renungkanlah pepatah Melayu agar tidak membakar kelambu sebab seekor nyamuk yang dimarahkan.

e04bf223ee11e1a3: SAN FRANCISCO: Amazon shares fell more than seven percent in after-hours trading Thursday following a quarterly earnings report that missed analyst expectations on profit and total revenue but showed strong growth in the company's AWS cloud business.
The miss came as investors were already rattled by Google's own lower-than-expected profits on a slowdown in advertising and big spending on AI.
Shares in Google-parent Alphabet dropped more than 10% after market close on Wednesday and closed down more than 12% on Thursday.
Intel meanwhile tumbled 20% after the bell Thursday after it said it expected a protracted slowdown for personal computers.
Amazon still expects to spend US$220 billion on capital expenditures this year, primarily on investments in artificial intelligence, it said.

The company recorded US$201.9 billion in total revenue and US$20.7 billion in profit in the third quarter, below expectations of US$202.2 billion and US$21.5 billion, respectively, according to FactSet.
Revenue from advertising services also fell short, reaching US$19.6 billion versus US$20.8 billion expected.

Amazon touted potentially lucrative business segments which extend beyond e-commerce, including grocery through Whole Foods, health care and pharmacy services, its Leo internet satellite division and Zoox autonomous vehicles.

"There has never been a trillion dollar revenue business, and we may have two of them in the next 5-10 years," CEO Andy Jassy said in a statement, echoing comments from July when he said that AWS was "booming."

The company is well-positioned to benefit from the artificial intelligence (AI) race due to its early lead in clouding computing services through AWS, which remains the top provider globally, followed by Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud.
Amazon said in July that its AI cloud and chips businesses each "exceeded" US$25 billion annual revenue run rates, a measure of recurring sales, representing "triple-digit" percentage growth.
Demand for its proprietary Trainium chips is "strong" and Amazon intends to make them more broadly available late next year, Jassy said on a call with analysts Thursday.
Debt load

Tech companies are expected to collectively spend hundreds of billions of dollars on AI-related expenses this year, which includes buying chips and building data centres, and investors are closely monitoring whether those investments are paying off.
Some companies have been taking on debt or raising cash through other means to fuel this growth.
Microsoft recently raised US$25 billion through a bond sale, according to reports on Thursday.
Alphabet, Meta, Nvidia and SpaceX have also borrowed billions over the past couple of years, contributing to AI-related debt reaching US$335 billion globally this year, according to Bloomberg.
Last week, Facebook-parent Meta said it would raise capital through a new stock offering, which will help fuel its AI spending.
Layoffs and buyouts
Tech companies have been trimming their global workforces in the name of efficiency, as well.
In January, Amazon said it would cut 16,000 jobs worldwide, its second major round of cuts after cutting 14,000 jobs last year.
Microsoft slashed close to four percent of its global workforce, impacting around 15,000 jobs, last year.
This week, Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to a quarter of its workforce, following an early retirement buyout offered to around seven percent of its employees earlier this year.
Netflix will reportedly cut around six percent of its workforce this year.
Auction site eBay laid off 1,000 employees earlier this month, more than doubling total layoffs this year.
In April, Meta said it would cancel plans to hire 6,000 people and also shift 7,000 other employees into AI workflow-related roles, then laid off around 10 percent of its global workforce in May.
Ride-hailing giant Uber said in September that it would lay off around 10 percent of its staff, impacting an estimated 3,000 or more employees.
685e78418a1cc59c: FRANKFURT: The European Central Bank on Thursday said it had crisis-fighting tools to deal with "disorderly" markets, seeking to calm worries that France's deteriorating public finances could shake the wider eurozone.

While the chances of the ECB intervening to help push down France's surging borrowing costs are currently seen as low, president Christine Lagarde's remarks appeared aimed at reassuring investors that policymakers would act if needed.

In a meeting just hours after Lagarde announced she would step down early, in February 2027, the central bank also kept its benchmark interest rate on hold despite rising inflation fuelled by the Iran war energy shock, but opened the door to another hike in December.

At a press conference after the decision, attention quickly shifted to France's debt woes after the country's bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, surged to their highest levels since 2002.

While declining to comment directly on the situation in France, Lagarde said that "should market developments threaten the smooth transmission of our monetary policy, including through unwarranted and disorderly market movements, we have instruments available to respond".
But she also appeared to downplay the chance of an imminent intervention, noting there were certain criteria to trigger such a step.

France's borrowing costs have risen sharply amid a standoff over attempts to push through a budget aiming to reduce the country's deficit and also after protests, driven in part by demands for more public spending, degenerated into the worst street violence in years.
There has been speculation that the ECB could, for the first time, use a crisis-fighting tool aimed at combating "disorderly" moves in sovereign debt markets.
However, the criteria to activate the yet-to-be-used Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) are strict, and most observers believe France's problems do not meet the threshold.
Lagarde has in the past reacted coolly when asked about the prospect of deploying the TPI.
While she did not go into detail about the subject on Thursday, she made general remarks about the need for eurozone member states to have sound public finances.
"Fiscal sustainability is a crucial anchor for broader economic stability," she said.
Hike debate
The rate decision came just hours after Lagarde announced she would step down in February next year, ahead of the official end of her term in October 2027.
This will allow European leaders to pick her successor before France's presidential elections in the spring, with officials fearing a far-right victory would complicate negotiations.
Lagarde gave little away about her next moves at Thursday's press conference, saying only she wanted to be able to speak more freely on matters outside of monetary policy.

This will stoke expectations that the former French finance minister, who served in centre-right governments, could campaign in the presidential elections, although she has previously ruled out running for the presidency herself.
The ECB's decision to hold rates steady, after two hikes earlier this year, was widely expected.

Eurozone inflation rose to a three-year high of 3.8% in September, driven by surging energy costs amid the Middle East conflict, but the ECB stressed core inflation -- excluding food and energy costs -- was under control.
"While the full effects of the energy shock are still unfolding, underlying inflation has remained broadly stable so far," Lagarde said.
She also justified the decision to keep rates on hold due to tighter financing conditions caused by rising bond yields.

Higher government yields can lead to increased borrowing costs for households and businesses, essentially having the same effect as higher interest rates -- and relieving the ECB of the need to increase rates further.
But Lagarde also revealed the ECB's governing council had "debated whether a hike was appropriate", fuelling expectations that rates could be increased at the central bank's next meeting in December.
She did little to dispel this notion, saying that "unless there were major developments, the direction of travel is quite clear".
d2679ddaa84ae4d4: WASHINGTON: The United States posted strong economic growth in the third quarter, but the Fed's preferred inflation gauge also accelerated, the commerce department said on Thursday, in a mixed economic bag for US president Donald Trump ahead of key midterm polls next week.
Real GDP increased at an annual rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, the department's Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) said in a statement, beating market expectations.

"The contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports," the BEA said in a statement.
The US Federal Reserve's preferred gauge for inflation -- the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index -- rose by 3.6% year-on-year in September, an increase from the previous month.

Trump's handling of the economy is a key issue for voters heading into midterm elections on Tuesday, where Democrats are seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress from the president's Republican Party.

The US-Israel war on Iran has sent global energy prices skyrocketing due to Tehran's retaliatory action, with US consumers paying an average of 42% more at the pump for regular gasoline, according to data from the AAA motor club.
The president's wide-ranging tariff policies have also upended global trade and fuelled inflation.
Strong GDP growth
The strong GDP growth will come as a boon to Trump, who has touted the strength of the economy despite the high prices that have posed a challenge to households across the country.

Much of the economic growth has been driven by an investment boom in Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology, which has seen companies spend billions on new models and in building the data centres that power them.
The BEA said the acceleration in GDP growth was driven by an increase in investment and an upturn in government spending, which were partially offset by a decrease in exports.
Imports -- which are a subtraction in the formula for GDP -- also increased more in the third quarter than the previous one.
Thursday's GDP data was an advance estimate released by the BEA, with two further estimates due in the coming weeks that could see the number revised.

Economists have warned for months that while US GDP growth has remained resilient despite price pressures from the war, outcomes have been highly uneven, with wealthier households prospering while working class families struggle.
Fed implications
The Fed prefers to use the PCE price index when gauging inflation, as it takes into account a broader range of household expenditures than Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation.
On Wednesday, the US central bank voted to keep interest rates steady, citing the need for more data to gauge how best to battle the surging inflation.
Chair Kevin Warsh reiterated the Fed's commitment to its long-term two-percent target for PCE inflation, which it has not achieved for more than five years.

He termed current inflation levels "too high" but cautioned against moving too quickly, saying the Fed had seen some tightening of financial conditions in response to the Fed raising interest rates in September -- its first hike in three years.
Markets largely expect the Fed to raise rates again by a quarter-point in December.
'Failed agenda'
Trump's political opponents slammed his handling of the economy over the quickening PCE figure, which showed a 21.3% year-on-year increase in the prices of energy goods and services.
"Today's data confirms families paid more in September for gasoline, housing, and health care," said Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren.
"Since Trump took office, families have paid US$3,772 on average because of inflation. Trump's failed agenda is driving up costs and eating into Americans' paychecks."
At a rally in South Carolina, Trump boasted about the "roaring" economy, renewed his attacks on Fed officials over monetary policy and told supporters to stick to voting Republican.
"If the Democrats win the midterms, they will burn it all down," he said.
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said the US economy was "on steroids right now" but that high inflation was its "Achilles heel."
"Growth came in stronger than expected and it's largely due to the massive AI business investment surge," she said. "The AI boom is adding almost a full percentage point to growth."
Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon, said spending by consumers was still high, but "they are increasingly stretching their budgets to afford pricier goods and services."

b36a902471af3eef: If you want to ask AI a question and watch the conversation go up in virtual flames when you're done, there's a new Mac app for that.

Howler is an open-source app from a Chinese developer going by Aries Zhou, and it takes incognito mode AI questions to a new level by making them graphically interesting and easy to access right from the desktop of a macOS device.

Anyone familiar with the Harry Potter series is likely to know where the name comes from - Howlers are letters that scream in recipients’ faces and then burst into flames, destroying themselves, which is the exact same thing the prompts ostensibly do once a user taps the Escape key.

The Howler app displays a parchment-esque letter on the screen whenever the user presses Option+H, complete with a little wax seal that shows a letter representing their chosen model. Responses to queries are written out “at a hand’s pace,” per Howler’s website, first in glowing gold that settles to a sepia-toned print.

“Besides needing translation at any time, I often want to look up a concept or learn about an event on the fly, without wanting to switch to a browser or open a separate session in Chat,” Zhou wrote in a comment on his Hacker News post showing off the applet. “So I made Howler, dedicated to Harry Potter fans, always there when you call, burning after reading.”

The biggest catch to using Howler is that setting it up involves either using an AI service that can run commands, like Claude Code or another coding agent, or running the configuration commands manually. The recommended method involves pasting a setup prompt into the agent's input field. Once set up, Howler can connect to supported AI models using an API key, or to compatible models running locally. Howler’s website states that the API key never enters the chat and is stored in the macOS Keychain for safety.

In addition to the API key for the chosen model staying local and not being printed, Howler is described on its website as only storing messages in memory with no history, sending requests straight to the chosen AI service and never through a relay, keeping no logs, and only connecting to an outside service to check for updates - and even that feature can be disabled.

It’s a handy tool for those who want to ask AI questions without leaving a chat history on their Mac – like trying to remember the name of that damn function you’re supposed to have down by now, or whether Memorial Day or Labor Day is the one in the fall. Just don’t assume the AI provider won’t retain a record of the exchange.

“Unlike regular conversations, it doesn't take up your conversation list, and you don't have to think about cleaning it up or archiving it afterward,” Zhou explained. “It's only for handling your sudden flashes of inspiration or a moment of confusion.”

And it does it with panache - sure, it’s just an interface for an AI model one could find elsewhere, but it’s easily conjured, dismissed with a snap, and is open source, to boot. You can find Howler on GitHub, or download it from its website, both linked above. ®

1905c7a2513a10b8: Vera Platforms, a startup founded by researchers at the University of Michigan, believes there's a way to make agents trustworthy enough to handle DevOps.

DevOps, which focuses on how software gets deployed and operated, is a particularly unforgiving affair. While AI agents have some leeway to make mistakes and correct errors as they generate code and work through a prompt, it's an entirely different matter when they make changes to real infrastructure running production workloads.

"Live infrastructure is unforgiving," Ang Chen, CEO of Vera Platforms and an associate professor at the University of Michigan, told The Register. "An incorrect change can take down a service, open a security hole or erase data. Mistakes are often irreversible, and there’s no safe way to experiment: running code against production infra just to see what happens isn’t an option."
For the past few years, Chen and his colleagues have been working on a way to benchmark agentic DevOps and a gym – a simulation environment – to help AI models get better at DevOps tasks.

"From the research that we did, we've figured out various weaknesses of leading models," said Chen. "For instance, [Anthropic's] Claude, although it's very strong with Python generation, it just has some fundamental limitations that it can't get right when it comes to DevOps."
An example of that, Chen said, is that when they asked Claude or OpenAI's Codex to decommission resources in the AWS cloud, the models didn't look beyond the default region.

"The default region is us-east-1," he explained. "There are various regions in AWS, but Claude doesn't have this awareness that the cloud resources could exist in multiple regions, so it only decommissioned part of the resource."
The fundamental reason, he said, is that these models have seen a lot of public code, but a lot less operational tracing.

Vera Platforms aims to remedy the situation with three products: vera-gym, a playground environment that emulates production infrastructure; vera-bench, a test for measuring where AI agents fumble DevOps tasks; and vera-agents, AI agents that have been trained in vera-gym and are ready to be deployed for DevOps tasks.

The CloudOpsBench test being released builds upon work done in 2024 that was presented at NeurIPS. According to Chen, Claude and Codex only score about a 50 percent pass rate. "It's a very, very hard set of tasks," he said.

The test covers tasks like deleting decommissioned S3 buckets, repairing a compliance event pipeline, and restoring DynamoDB write autoscaling. "The tasks are authored by senior infra operators with many years of experience, with rigorous peer review," said Chen.
This benchmark has the advantage of not requiring an actual cloud deployment.

"We have a high fidelity simulator that mimics Amazon behavior," said Chen. "So the rollout, the performance of the agent on the real cloud and the performance of the agent in our emulator is exactly the same. So for every API, we have this comparison and the agent sees the same thing."
Vera-agents, Chen said, should be available in Q1 2027.
In their academic work, the researchers describe cloud infrastructure as "critical but tedious work." With a bit more training, maybe AI agents can take over and keep things boring. ®
