fdc9c053616efe5d: You've probably heard, at this point, about the big changes coming to Meta's AI scraping terms for business accounts. Nieman Lab had that scoop, and since then, small businesses, journalists, and artists using Meta products like Instagram have been raising the alarm. But if you're in the EU or UK, you might be in luck and can object to that use of your data, as some users have pointed out.
If You're In the UK or EU, Here's How to Object to Meta's AI Training

Earlier this month, Meta updated its commercial terms of use for business accounts to allow it to “use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta’s products.

Many artists and small business owners that rely on Instagram and Facebook are livid at Meta granting itself permission to use their content, including from websites simply connected to their Meta accounts, to train AI. But for users in the United Kingdom and European Union, for now, there’s a way to object.

Meta buried this change in its Commercial Terms, and Nieman Lab first reported on the change. The update was originally set to go into effect on October 30, but following backlash, Meta changed the effective date to November 20. Adding to the confusion, Meta then removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases, Nieman Lab reported, and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” where previously it said that data would be used for all Meta products. Those terms still allow Meta plenty of leeway for scraping users’ data to develop its products, however.

Several users based in the UK and EU have explained how to object on Instagram. On mobile: by clicking the three lines on their account, going to the privacy center, and clicking “object,” which goes to a form that asks users to write why they are objecting to their data being used. They received an email from Meta saying their objections were approved.
On the podcast this week, we talk Flock CEO’s leaked police conference audio and Sam’s piece about Marissa Mayer’s latest meltdown. Subscribe wherever you get your pods.

The New York Times has an antisocial aversion to linking: Another day, another the-New-York-Times-isn’t-linking controversy. The specifics here almost don’t matter because this happens seemingly every day, but basically the New York Times investigation about chemical plant polluters under the Trump administration was covered in much the same way by Hunterbrook, a news outlet fused with a hedge fund. The Times article—which led the Sunday print edition—uses similar photos, some of the same sources, and covers similar ground to Hunterbrook’s earlier investigation from February, with no acknowledgment or link whatsoever. After the cofounder of Hunterbrook rightfully ranted about this on X, the Times added an acknowledgment (but no link!!!) toward the bottom of the story. Puck’s Dylan Byers has a good rundown about what happened, which includes parts of a three-paragraph Times’ spokesperson statement explaining at length why they don’t think they have to link. This is extremely antisocial, deranged behavior and it’s ridiculous that the Times is still getting away with this. Bottom line: I’m sure the Times was already working on this story, what with their massive newsroom. Even so, they got beat, and they should link. Journalism awards need to stop looking the other way when big outlets do this. This has happened to us many times and it actually does matter for smaller outlets and links are free. Let’s try them!

Artificial reef: TIL that a gigantic military ship, the SS United, is going to be purposefully sunk to be turned into an “artificial reef.” Scuba divers seem quite excited. I didn’t really know that this was a thing that was done, but maybe I’m a rube.

Now Kalshi is finding new ways to put a price on those predictions. This partnership between Kalshi and S&P Dow Jones Indices is fascinating.” C’mon, man.

The scrapes were likely automated. But that is exactly the problem: as far as our logs show, nobody checked. b65bd78dcb9b0242: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Earlier this month, Meta updated its commercial terms of use for business accounts to allow it to “use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta’s products.

Many artists and small business owners that rely on Instagram and Facebook are livid at Meta granting itself permission to use their content, including from websites simply connected to their Meta accounts, to train AI. But for users in the United Kingdom and European Union, for now, there’s a way to object.

Meta buried this change in its Commercial Terms, and Nieman Lab first reported on the change. The update was originally set to go into effect on October 30, but following backlash, Meta changed the effective date to November 20. Adding to the confusion, Meta then removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases, Nieman Lab reported, and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” where previously it said that data would be used for all Meta products. Those terms still allow Meta plenty of leeway for scraping users’ data to develop its products, however.

EU users’ personal data rights are governed by the General Data Protection Regulation and the AI Act. GDPR, which became enforceable in 2018, requires explicit consent to use personal data. This includes the right to object to one’s data being used. The AI Act, which went into effect in 2024, dictates how AI companies can use personal data, and how people can opt in or out, stating that they can withdraw consent at any time. The UK has its own version of the GDPR. The European Commission states: “The GDPR rules only apply to personal data about individuals; they do not govern data about companies or any other legal entities. However, information in relation to companies may constitute personal data where it allows the identification of a natural person.”

Several users based in the UK and EU have explained how to object on Instagram. Instagram user bookish.sil posted a walkthrough of how they did it on mobile: by clicking the three lines on their account, going to the privacy center, and clicking “object,” which goes to a form that asks users to write why they are objecting to their data being used. They received an email from Meta saying their objection was approved. Instagram user jenniqueart posted a similar walkthrough with the same results.

My Meta accounts are based in the US, but using a VPN to locate my IP address in London, I could see options in my Meta privacy settings that would let me object to the use of my information by Meta AI. To get there on desktop with a VPN on, I went to my account privacy center, clicked “Submit a privacy rights request” at the bottom, selected Instagram, clicked “How can I object to the processing of my information?” and got to a page where I could choose to object to the use of my information for Meta AI or third parties, which were two separate options.
When my location is based in the US, these options don't appear.

When I clicked through the option to “object to the use of my information for Meta AI,” however, it returned an error page that said “This form is only available to people in certain regions.” GDPR is meant to apply to wherever someone is located at the time, but since this objection applies to the preferences of one account, it might be based on where the account was created. I tried again located in Belgium and got the same results. I’ve asked Meta to clarify.

As many have already pointed out in the comments on UK and EU users who’ve posted walkthroughs, these objection steps aren’t available to people outside of those countries, and as Meta continuously changes its platform, these steps might not work for everyone always. Unless something changes before November 20, the rest of us are screwed.
c11769620a3fa457: Security is the dominant feature of the EU's new Arctic strategy. dotshock / ShutterstockThe EU recently presented its latest Arctic strategy. It is the bloc’s fifth such strategy since 2008 and the first to be published since 2021, a few months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. This conflict has disrupted Arctic governance. The work of the Arctic Council, which includes Russia as one of its eight member states, was paused shortly after the invasion. The council is the primary forum for cooperation in the region. Since 2022, the Russian security threat in the Arctic has also grown. Russia has engaged in hybrid activities in the region, ranging from disinformation operations and GPS jamming to the targeting of pipelines and undersea cables. The EU’s new strategy has four priorities: strengthening peace, security and resilience in the Arctic, addressing climate change, delivering economic development and ensuring regional and social development for Arctic communities. These priorities are broadly in line with the previous 2021 strategy, in which geopolitical issues were already more present than in earlier years. But there are several major changes. More security and less climate action A word count reveals the profound impact the deteriorating cooperation context has had on the EU’s stance on the region. In the latest update, the word “security” is mentioned 52 times compared with 23 times in 2021. By contrast, “climate change” appears only 14 times in the new strategy compared with 30 times previously. This shift towards security is a general trend in the Arctic since 2022. The creation of an annual Arctic Security Conference in 2024, which discusses security trends in the region, is an example of this. Security also figures prominently in recently published national Arctic strategies, including France, Italy, Germany and Sweden. Climate change is not completely absent from the EU’s latest Arctic strategy, and the bloc reaffirmed its commitment to combat it in the document. But, where previously climate change was the cornerstone of the EU’s Arctic engagement, it is now presented through a security lens. Climate change is identified as “amplifying security risks” and a “defining threat” from which Arctic inhabitants need to be “protected”. Security shapes all four priorities of the new strategy. Arctic communities also get much more attention than in earlier documents. Although the inclusion of Indigenous people also figures more prominently, the conflation between Indigenous and local people has previously been criticised by the Saami Council. The conflation undermines the specific rights and distinct interests of Indigenous groups such as the Sámi. A ‘northern neighbourhood’ Another key change in the EU’s new Arctic strategy is the introduction of the concept of a “northern neighbourhood”. The name suggests similarities with the EU’s European Neighbourhood Policy, which it launched in 2004 to foster closer ties with its eastern and southern neighbours. But it is unclear what exact form the northern neighbourhood will take. The northern neighbourhood is not presented as a new multilateral institution. Instead, it has been put forward as a political framework enabling cooperation projects and integration between the EU and “like-minded” partners such as Greenland, Norway, Iceland, Canada and the UK. By excluding Russia, this new political framework signals a change in the EU’s understanding of the Arctic. The EU’s early engagement in the region came from a will to extend European integration to the east and north in the 2000s. The Arctic was also an area where cooperation with Russia was possible, despite disagreements elsewhere. The concept of a northern neighbourhood reveals a geographical shift in focus towards Greenland and the west and north Atlantic more generally. Yet while the US is still listed among the potential members of the northern neighbourhood, it comes with implicit conditions. According to the new strategy, a partnership with the US needs to be “predictable” and based on “shared interests and values”. This is reminiscent of the language that prevailed for Russia in the previous policies. What kind of power is the EU? Perhaps the biggest change in the new strategy lies in the document’s affirmation that multilateral cooperation “can no longer be the sole foundation of the EU’s Arctic approach”. This means two things. First, that multilateralism is no longer the prominent form of cooperation in the Arctic. And second, that the EU’s geopolitical stance in general is changing from being the champion and embodiment of multilateralism to another form of power. This is also visible in the emphasis the new strategy puts on the EU’s material capabilities and infrastructures as conditions for security. It includes mention of, among other things, developing Europe’s capacity to build icebreaker vessels. The EU’s new Arctic strategy signals a broad shift in the European geopolitical mindset. Climate change and multilateralism have been overshadowed by security concerns due to the fractured Arctic geopolitical landscape. However, ultimately, climate change and social concerns will remain key priorities of Arctic inhabitants and the EU should not lose sight of this. ad8a7bfc37201941: Patients who think they're getting an annual checkup often end up with an unexpected bill. The Good Brigade/DigitalVision Collection via Getty ImagesI was teaching health economics when a student raised his hand. We were discussing the Affordable Care Act, or ACA, which requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services at no additional cost to patients. I explained that preventive care could cost nothing. The student had expected that, too. Instead, he said, he received a bill for more than US$500 after his checkup. He was so frustrated that he said he would never go back for another annual checkup. I suggested he contact his insurer to find out why he had been charged and whether his visit had been billed as preventive care. Then another student spoke up. Her husband had paid several hundred dollars for what he thought would be a free checkup too. The very next day, I received a $78 bill for my own Pap smear. I expected my insurance to cover this cervical cancer screening without cost-sharing because it is among the preventive services recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force and generally covered under the ACA. When I called my insurer, I learned that the visit had been billed as a regular outpatient office visit, with no mention of the Pap smear. I then called my primary care provider’s office. The clinic acknowledged a coding error and corrected it. My bill dropped to zero. As an assistant professor of health policy and addiction studies at Penn State Harrisburg, I know whom to call and what questions to ask when I receive an unexpected medical bill. Many of my graduate students worked full time and took evening classes. Would they know how to dispute a bill, or have time? Those experiences led me to investigate how often patients pay out of pocket for annual checkups. I teamed up with fellow researchers Erin Duffy and Max Crowley to examine this question. In our analysis of a Pennsylvania survey, nearly 1 in 4 insured respondents reported paying for their most recent checkup. Why a preventive visit may come with a bill Many health care services covered by insurance are subject to copayments or deductibles. A copayment is a fixed amount patients pay for a covered service, while a deductible is the amount they generally must pay for covered care before insurance starts paying. The ACA, however, requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services, including screenings for high blood pressure and certain cancers, vaccinations and counseling to help people quit smoking. These should come at no cost to patients. Generally, this applies when patients see providers who are in their insurance plan’s network. But that doesn’t mean every annual checkup is free. If a patient discusses a new symptom or asks the clinician to manage an existing condition during their annual checkup, it can result in a separate office-visit charge. A test may be billed as diagnostic rather than preventive, and coverage varies by plan and provider. Sometimes, as in my case, a coding error is responsible. Not every charge is inappropriate. The challenge is that patients often cannot tell which services should be covered, why they were billed, or whether a mistake occurred. What our survey found Previous studies have found, using insurance claims, that patients sometimes face out-of-pocket costs during preventive visits. But these records show how visits were billed, not necessarily what patients believed they were receiving. We wanted to know whether people who thought they were getting annual checkups also reported paying out of pocket. Our study, published in August 2026 in the peer-reviewed journal Prevention Science, used the 2024 Penn State Lion Poll, an online survey of Pennsylvania adults. We analyzed responses from 912 insured adults who reported an annual checkup within the preceding 10 years. Most had one in the past year. Of those respondents, 23.5% reported paying out of pocket for their most recent checkup. Among those who paid, the average reported out-of-pocket amount was $68.50. After accounting for other characteristics such as age, gender, insurance type, income and education, we found that respondents who were not familiar with ACA preventive-care protections were about 12 percentage points more likely to report paying than those who were familiar with the protections. That difference is equivalent to roughly 12 more people paying out of every 100. Those who considered healthcare unaffordable were about 13 percentage points more likely to pay than those who found it affordable. Because our survey relied on patients’ reports rather than billing records, we could not determine why individual charges occurred, or whether they were appropriate. The findings show associations, not causation, and our nonrandom sample cannot provide a precise statewide estimate. How doctor visits are billed doesn’t always match what service patients think they are receiving. adamkaz/E+ Collection via Getty Images Why these bills matter I kept thinking about the student who said he would never return for another checkup. Research has shown that even modest out-of-pocket costs can discourage people from getting recommended screenings. Delaying preventive care could mean missing opportunities to detect health problems early, when treatment may be more effective. Our survey did not find a statistically significant association between paying for a previous checkup and planning another one. However, respondents who were unfamiliar with ACA protections or considered healthcare unaffordable were less likely to plan a checkup. These findings suggest that uncertainty about costs may discourage people from seeking preventive care. What patients can do Before a visit, ask your insurer which preventive services are covered without cost-sharing and confirm that your provider is in-network. Ask the clinic whether discussing other health concerns or receiving additional tests could trigger a charge. If a bill arrives, compare it with your insurer’s explanation of benefits, which you can typically find in your online insurance account or receive by mail. Ask the provider’s billing office which services and codes were submitted and request a correction if something appears wrong. You can also contact your insurer to question or appeal a coverage decision. A colleague told me she challenged a $20 or $30 copayment requested at check-in for an annual visit after remembering our conversations. The charge was removed. Patients should not have to become experts in insurance billing to receive preventive care. Clearer coverage information and more transparent billing could help people seek care without fearing unexpected costs. 1084f4473e021767: Paying for childcare remains one of the biggest costs for households, often costing as much as housing. AP Photo/Craig MitchelldyerWhile affordability pressures are hitting Americans in many facets of their lives, from groceries to gas prices to housing costs, one important expense often gets less attention – childcare. After a huge infusion of federal funds into childcare dried up at the end of the Biden administration, experts warned that this sharp cutoff, sometimes dubbed the “childcare cliff,” would force parents to either scale back work to handle the extra caretaking or pay steep costs out of pocket. The potential effects of the federal cuts are hard to estimate, in part because states took different approaches in the aftermath. In some cases, they offset the sharp cuts in part by redirecting other funds to childcare. But several states, including Vermont, New Mexico and Kentucky, have gone further and innovated on their own to shore up support for working parents and their young children. Meanwhile, New York City is expanding free toddler slots for lower-income families, following Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s announcement to build a universal early childcare system. Taken together, these experiments point to bipartisan ways to support working parents, especially if the results of the November 2026 midterms signal a new willingness to tackle one of the biggest cost burdens for families. As researchers of sociology and childcare policy with six children from 1 to 16 years old between us, we have also gained insights from our own data gathered over 75 interviews with parents in St. Louis, Missouri, over the past few years. We see them struggling with a fragmented childcare system that’s in need of a deep strategic investment. These families face limited choices and soaring costs for an essential good that allows a parent to go to work. Out-of-pocket expenses for parents using center-based care in childcare centers and private preschool programs have more than doubled since 2019. In 2024, the national average price of childcare was US$13,128 annually, which rivals housing as the most expensive item in family budgets. States go their own way The disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic laid bare the critical role that reliable, high-quality childcare plays for working families. But we believe it also presented an opportunity for innovative investments in the nation’s fractured childcare landscape. Pandemic relief legislation in 2021 directed nearly $40 billion to shore up the supply and quality of childcare. This funding increase, which was a fourfold jump over previous levels, supported childcare staff with higher wages and allowed for other investments to improve the quality of care. The reach was vast, with stabilization funds flowing to 220,000 providers serving 9.6 million children. Many states also provided grants to create new slots and improve how providers got paid. As those funds began drying up in September 2023, some states started to address these shortfalls on their own. In some cases, they took significant steps at a policy level to channel more support to working parents. We believe these investments could serve as examples for the rest of the country. One is Vermont, which in 2023 became the first state to pass a law establishing a childcare entitlement. Following more than a decade of advocacy and bipartisan support, the law established a near-universal public childcare system, funded partially through a payroll tax of 0.44% split between employers and employees. Through an expansion of subsidies along income tiers, the number of families covered rose by 55% from July 2022 to May 2025, while flexible grants increased the number of providers and focused on improving the quality of care. About 12,000 children are now covered under this program. New Mexico went even further. In November 2025, the state became the first in the nation to offer universal childcare. Based on an older program that provided free childcare to low-income families, the initiative expanded support to all working parents regardless of income. Children draw at a daycare center in Albuquerque, N.M., which has gone further than any other state in expanding subsidies for working parents. AP Photo/Susan Montoya Bryan Before the expansion, 32,000 children were covered, a number the state aims to double by 2028. On average, the state estimates that the program will save families $12,000 a year. Meanwhile, the Kentucky legislature in April 2026 passed a measure with strong bipartisan support to make major investments in the state’s childcare infrastructure. Key provisions include free childcare for the children of childcare center employees, increased state-subsidized reimbursement rates, and required training to support very young special needs children. The Kentucky measure also loosened regulations that had made it tough for employers to share costs for care, such as renting facilities, while pitching a pilot program to open one-room “microcenters” in communities that lacked sufficient childcare options. In addition, Gov. Andy Beshear launched a complementary Pre-K for All pilot program in several counties. Another example is New York City, where Mamdani has announced an expansion for toddlers as young as 2 years old in all five of the city’s boroughs, building on the city’s programs for free childcare for 3-K and pre-K. To date, this effort has increased some slots, although the rollout in September hit bumps. The childcare crunch by the numbers Given the skyrocketing costs, over 70% of families who sought care say it’s difficult to find childcare – and that doesn’t count the 11% who fail to find any at all, according to a 2023 government survey. That report found that families with Black or Hispanic children or infants, and those living in the South and West, are more likely to run into cost as a barrier. On the supply side, three-quarters of providers say they have to turn many families away or put them on waiting lists. Center-based care for an infant costs more than in-state college tuition at a public university in 32 states, yet childcare workers, who are overwhelmingly women of color, earn the same as parking lot attendants and dog walkers. That makes them some of the lowest-paid workers in the entire economy. Amid soaring costs and scarce supply, roughly half of all U.S. families live in so-called childcare deserts – areas where there are three children under 5 for every licensed-care slot. The answer for many families in these cases is to rely on ad hoc and irregular informal care. Some parents told us they’re turning to relatives and neighbors for help. Others resorted to using unlicensed, and potentially unsafe, childcare providers because they found no other viable options. And for some remote workers, the daunting solution is to care for their kids themselves while working. The problem with such makeshift arrangements is that they tend, on average, to offer fewer of the learning opportunities linked to children’s long-term development and social mobility. And even these arrangements can be tough to afford: One single mother we interviewed told us she paid for a week’s childcare in kind with her own breast milk, which went to feed the care provider’s grandchildren. We also spoke to parents who reported choosing between childcare bills and heat, electricity or rent. Another mom told us about a more unconventional solution. She and her husband work full time but can’t afford the childcare options in their community, so she decided to join a gym that provides free childcare while its members exercise. She brings her laptop and works, rather than working out, while her toddler plays. These parents are scraping by in the absence of the affordable, subsidized childcare options commonplace in other countries. But this crunch is also a lose-lose proposition for the economy. The U.S. could lose as much as $290 billion per year by 2030 in forgone economic activity due to women not working or not working as much due to childcare pressures, according to the consultancy BCG. A path forward The Trump administration has laid out its own vision. Vice President JD Vance announced in September 2026 a preliminary proposal to repurpose existing funds for childcare subsidies as a cash transfer to married parents, provided that one spouse stays home. We believe, however, this approach fails to reflect the real needs of the millions of U.S. parents who can’t pay their bills if they only get one paycheck. In fact, under the subsidy program that Vance cited, only 16% of eligible children are reached today anyway. We believe, based on our research, that any comprehensive overhaul has four important components. First is a robust national policy for paid family leave, which would let families make the best care decisions for newborns, infants and parents themselves rather than sprinting back to work. Paid family leave would also ease demand for scarce infant care in the market. Second is an expansion of early childhood care and education programs. By publicly subsidizing childcare, particularly for low-income families and special needs kids, policymakers can help close the affordability gap for high-quality care. Third is a greater investment in childcare workers. Qualified caregivers are the cornerstone of high-quality childcare. If their wages and working conditions improve, it means fewer will have to take side hustles or quit for better jobs. Finally, providers will need more incentives to open in underserved areas. Childcare is expensive to provide and runs on thin margins. In low-income and rural areas, many families can’t pay prices that cover the true cost of care, and subsidy payments are often set below that cost. So opening a center there doesn’t make much financial sense. Startup grants, higher subsidy rates and operating support help close that gap, which makes it possible to open and stay open where need is greatest. 04f101fb6f68cf59: If you're going with a lower-cost health insurance plan, make sure to read the fine print. Pla2na/iStock via Getty Images PlusHealthcare costs are a major concern for Americans, and health insurance premiums are a primary fuel for that anxiety. Shrinking federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans led to large premium increases for millions of Americans in 2025, causing many people to drop coverage. With premiums expected to rise further and Medicaid work requirements set to begin in January 2027, many Americans are left scrambling for affordable options. We are health economists who study public policies aimed at expanding health insurance coverage. When it comes to our own health insurance, we are fortunate: We are among the roughly 160 million Americans who receive coverage through their employers. But if you don’t work for a large employer that provides health benefits, finding coverage for your family can be confusing and, increasingly, expensive. People looking for low-cost alternatives have no doubt encountered several options. They may look appealing and, in some cases, may be appropriate, but they can also carry real risks. Navigating trade-offs Historically, people who didn’t have access to employer-sponsored coverage had limited health insurance options. Before the Affordable Care Act went into effect in 2014, insurers could charge you a higher premium based on your health status, exclude coverage for preexisting medical conditions, or deny you coverage altogether. The ACA eliminated this kind of discrimination, established a minimum standard of 10 essential benefits that health insurance plans had to cover, and required plans to fully cover the cost of preventive care. It also introduced income-based subsidies that could be used to purchase coverage in newly established online marketplaces. Americans who are not insured through an employer-sponsored plan must find coverage through sources like the ACA marketplaces. mixetto/E+ via Getty Images Low-cost plans that aren’t available through ACA marketplaces are essentially vestiges of the pre-ACA health insurance landscape. Regardless of where you get coverage, choosing health insurance involves trade-offs. The more you pay in premiums, the more comprehensive your coverage will be in terms of how much you must pay when you need care and the breadth of the network of covered providers. Some trade-offs are clear when you choose a plan, but some lower-cost options may have limitations that are not immediately obvious. Less costly short-term plans As their name suggests, short-term, limited-duration plans are designed for people with temporary gaps in coverage, such as those who are between jobs or months away from qualifying for Medicare. These plans, which can be purchased for periods of up to six months, tend to be cheaper than marketplace coverage for two reasons. First, because they are not subject to ACA rules, they may not provide the full range of essential health benefits. Short-term, limited-duration plans often do not cover maternity care and commonly don’t have an annual limit on out-of-pocket costs. In fact, these plans may cap how much they will pay in a year, leaving policyholders stuck with large, unexpected expenses. Second, unlike plans offered through the ACA marketplaces, short-term, limited-duration plans are allowed to deny coverage based on your health status. Screening out higher-cost consumers reduces premiums, but if you are not in perfect health, you may not be able to find an insurer that will sell you one of these more limited plans. Because of a concern that they destabilize the market by siphoning off healthy consumers, short-term, limited-duration plans are banned in five states. Alternatives that look like insurance Another seemingly affordable option is healthcare sharing ministries, arrangements through which consumers with common religious beliefs agree to share medical expenses. Their websites resemble those of health insurance companies – for example, they often present different plan options offering different levels of benefits – but they avoid using standard insurance terms like “premium” or “deductible” because these offerings are not insurance. Because they are not regulated as insurance companies, healthcare sharing ministries are not subject to consumer protections or other state or federal requirements. There is also no guarantee that the ministry will cover your medical expenses when you submit a claim. Like short-term, limited-duration plans, healthcare sharing ministries may deny coverage based on your health history, exclude coverage for preexisting conditions and put a limit on the dollar amount they will pay in benefits. Another lower-cost option available in 14 states is health coverage offered by a farm bureau. These plans are similar to healthcare sharing ministries in that they are limited to a certain group of people – to enroll, you must be a member of the state’s farm bureau, though that does not mean you necessarily have to work in agriculture. These plans are also not subject to federal or state insurance regulations. This means that, like short-term, limited-duration plans, they can offer lower prices by not offering certain benefits required by the ACA and by screening out high-cost consumers. Unlike short-term, limited-duration plans, there is no limit on how long you can hold farm bureau coverage. Choosing a health insurance plan often requires fighting through a thicket of jargon. What should you do? Although the cost of marketplace coverage has increased dramatically since 2025, for many consumers who need coverage for more than six months, it remains the best option. If you are single with an annual income below US$64,000, a couple with an annual income below $87,000, or a family of four with an annual income less than $132,000, you should still be eligible for a premium subsidy. And you will know that the plan you are purchasing is real insurance that covers a standard set of benefits and is subject to robust consumer protections. If you are considering an alternative to marketplace coverage, there are a few things you should do to protect yourself: Make sure you ask for a summary of benefits and coverage. This is a plain language summary of a health plan’s benefits and coverage with examples of how much the plan would cover for two specific conditions – diabetes and childbirth. Insurers and employers who offer coverage are required to provide this document to anyone applying for coverage. If they cannot provide one, what they are selling may not actually be insurance. If they do provide a summary of benefits and coverage, read it carefully. As we noted earlier, one reason some options might be less expensive than a marketplace plan is that they provide much less coverage. Don’t assume that they cover all the benefits you would expect from a health insurance plan, or that they will cover the full cost of the care you receive. Finally, never enter your phone number into a “do you need insurance” website. This area is rife with fraud, including multiple cases in which telemarketers misled consumers into paying hundreds of dollars per month to purchase sham health insurance. Health insurance is expensive because healthcare is expensive – which means that consumers have to make difficult trade-offs. There is no easy answer, but beware of options that look too good to be true. They very well might be. Thomas Buchmueller is a Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. He was part of a team that received state funding from 2015 to 2022 to evaluate the Healthy Michigan Plan, Michigan's ACA Medicaid expansion. In 2011-2012 he was the Senior Health Economist at the White House Council of Economic Advisers and from 2023-2025 he was Deputy Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Helen Levy was part of a team that received state funding from 2015 to 2022 to evaluate the Healthy Michigan Plan, Michigan's ACA Medicaid expansion. She served as a Senior Economist at the White House Council of Economic Advisers in 2010-2011.
119cf39f6711bef0: Many of the stores where people use SNAP benefits are small. O2O Creative/E+ via Getty ImagesAfter 10 states began to add new restrictions to what people could buy with Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits in early 2026, the number of convenience stores authorized to accept those benefits was 1.4% lower than would be expected based on trends in states without the policy change. That’s what we found in our study, published in October 2026 in Health Affairs Scholar – a peer-reviewed journal. SNAP, a federally funded program administered by the states, helps about 36 million low-income Americans afford groceries with government benefits that can be used at more than 250,000 stores to buy fresh fruit, ground beef, canned beans and other groceries. Using the benefits for many items, including hot food, alcohol, toiletries and pet food, has long been prohibited. States can now obtain federal waivers to prohibit SNAP benefits from being used to buy other products. The 10 states with waivers that we studied had a mix of rules. Some only barred the sale of soda and other sugary drinks. Other prohibitions applied to energy drinks, candy, cake and other prepared desserts. In states like Oklahoma and Florida that have adopted these new SNAP restrictions to discourage unhealthy diets, the number of convenience stores participating in the program has fallen relative to other states that haven’t made these changes. That was especially notable in areas with high numbers of low-income people where a large share of the population gets SNAP benefits. We analyzed the number of stores participating in SNAP from January 2025 through June 2026 for the 10 states. We compared changes to that number before and after the waivers took effect with what happened in the rest of the country. We found no clear evidence that the number of supermarkets or superstores was declining in waiver states. Although it’s slightly lower than otherwise expected, this effect is not statistically significant. Because the restrictions vary, we also investigated whether the type mattered: sugary drinks only, or sugary drinks plus other products that state officials wanted to discourage. We found the largest declines in the number of SNAP-authorized convenience stores in states restricting both drinks and candy: an average of 2.2%. Why it matters Stores in waiver states may need to update their checkout systems and train employees to prevent purchases that are no longer allowed with SNAP benefits – potentially a time-consuming burden for some retailers. That may help explain why the number of SNAP-authorized convenience stores is declining. Although most people use SNAP benefits to buy food at big stores, they also purchase some groceries at convenience stores, especially in neighborhoods where there are few supermarkets. Other federal policies are also changing how SNAP works due to provisions in the big tax and policy legislation that Congress passed in July 2025. It changed some eligibility rules and how much states pay to administer the program. Even before all those changes take effect, many people who are likely eligible for SNAP benefits are having a harder time getting them, due to the steps states are taking to prepare for the new rules. The number of Americans enrolled in the program is falling fast despite no sign that their needs are shrinking. What still isn’t known We focused on changes to the number of stores authorized to accept SNAP in states with waivers. We didn’t study whether stores closed, or exactly why stores left the program. We also don’t know what role court rulings will play. On June 22, near the end of our study, a federal court invalidated SNAP food restrictions in five states: Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee and West Virginia. Waiver programs in other states – Indiana, Utah, Idaho, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Texas and Florida – were allowed to continue. Four states had similar restrictions in the works: South Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio and Virginia. Those plans are on hold. Beginning in November 2026, most U.S. stores will also have to meet new requirements of a different kind to participate in SNAP. They’ll need to stock a wider variety of staple foods, such as grains, dairy products and produce. These requirements could pose additional challenges for convenience stores. Further research is needed to see if the effects we found change over time, including in states that introduce these restrictions after the period we studied. The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work. Justin White receives funding from Bloomberg Philanthropies’ Food Policy Program. a94cb7158a379b67: Amber Titus, 38, holds a take-home dose of methadone on Sept. 18 in Bisbee Junction, Ariz. Daniela Dawson, CC BY-NDThree times a week, Amber Titus wakes up at 5 a.m. to get ready for the 45-minute drive to the methadone clinic. Titus, 38, and her husband live with their two young children in Bisbee Junction, Arizona, a rural community near the U.S.-Mexico border. The couple started taking methadone, a medication that treats opioid addiction, in early 2025. “It’s been a godsend,” she said. But accessing methadone is not easy. The closest place they can receive treatment is a clinic in Sierra Vista, about 30 miles from their home. The clinic opens on weekdays at 4:30 a.m. but closes before midday. Titus has to get her methadone dose and arrive at work in Bisbee before her shift starts at 9 a.m. Arriving just 10 to 15 minutes late for an appointment can mean missing a dose because rules are so strict, she said, even when the clinic is still open. Like many people with opioid use disorder, Amber Titus struggles to access methadone treatment. Three times a week, she drives 45 minutes each way with her 1-year-old son in his car seat to get the medication. Here’s her story. That’s the routine when they have their own transportation. In August, their car was totaled in a crash. Until they got another one, Titus called Medicaid, her insurance provider, to schedule rides to the clinic. “They said they’d be at my house at 6 o'clock in the morning,” Titus told The Conversation. The driver was late every day. “I missed my methadone dose for the whole week,” she said. Nationwide, more than 120 people a day died from opioid overdoses in 2025, according to federal estimates. Methadone is one of the most effective medications for opioid use disorder, cutting the risk of fatal overdose by roughly half. Yet only 22% of people with the disorder ever receive it. For more than five decades, only specialized, government-approved clinics, known as opioid treatment programs, have dispensed methadone, not regular doctors or pharmacies. Many clinics require patients to show up in person every single day, with average one-way drive times approaching 50 minutes in rural communities. Today, private equity firms have acquired large shares of the market for methadone clinics, telling lawmakers their capital has expanded treatment and modernized care. I am a healthcare economist at Brown University who studies how private equity is reshaping American medicine. My recent research on private equity’s growing footprint in addiction treatment, co-authored with researchers from the University of Pittsburgh and RAND, found that despite acquiring over one-third of methadone clinics in the U.S., private equity investments have not expanded methadone availability or the construction of new facilities. This research has informed federal investigations into the role of private equity in expanding access to medications for addiction treatment. Currently, U.S. Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., has an investigation into three of the country’s largest methadone clinic operators, citing concerns that they oppose expanding treatment access for financial reasons rather than patient safety. Why methadone fits the private equity model Because methadone is so tightly regulated, opioid treatment programs are, in effect, a government-created monopoly. In most of the country, if you want methadone, there’s a short list of clinics licensed to give it to you and no other way to get it. Moreover, people with opioid use disorder generally must travel to opioid treatment programs every day, where staff must observe them taking methadone, with strict limits on how much methadone patients can take home and when they can do so. Take-home methadone varies based on the state, time in treatment and clinician discretion. Only 19% of people who received take-home methadone received three or more days’ supply. That kind of guaranteed, captive demand is exactly the sort of investment that can be profitable for private equity investors. Whoever controls the clinics in a region controls access to the medication and can set the terms for patients in most need of medication. Private equity firms have invested more than US$1 trillion in U.S. healthcare over the past two decades, touching everything from fertility clinics to hospice care. Many Americans have never heard the term private equity, but these firms now own more than 400 U.S. hospitals and oversee doctors in more than a quarter of the country’s emergency rooms. In opioid treatment specifically, firms have used a platform and add-on strategy: buying one large clinic, then steadily acquiring smaller nearby ones, similar to a company quietly buying up every gas station in a county until, years later, one owner controls them all. Individually, each deal looks too small to matter. Collectively, a single firm can end up controlling an entire region’s methadone supply. To be clear, private investment isn’t inherently harmful. Research shows that in markets where quality is easy to see, competition is robust and there’s no government subsidy – restaurants, for instance – private equity can have neutral or even positive effects. Healthcare has none of those features. Patients often can’t judge provider quality, they rarely pay for care directly, and government programs act as both payer and regulator. Market share grew, methadone supply didn’t My research has quantified what actually happened after private equity acquisitions of opioid treatment programs. Previous research I have done, which my ongoing work builds upon, examined acquisitions from 2011 to 2019 and found that within two years of a private equity firm moving into a county, it typically controlled 67% of the local methadone treatment market – and in more than a quarter of counties, a single firm controlled all of it. Despite acquiring that much market power, these acquisitions generally do not result in the construction of new methadone clinics or an increase in methadone treatment. Additionally, the data shows that methadone shipments, or what clinics have to dispense to patients, and opioid-related deaths were unchanged during the study period. In plain terms: Private equity firms haven’t been building new capacity – they’ve been buying up the capacity that already existed. As of October 2026, there are 1,572 methadone clinics registered with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Nationally, 35% of opioid treatment providers are affiliated with private equity firms, and in 19 states and the District of Columbia more than half have private equity owners. Montana has four clinics, all owned by Community Medical Services, more commonly known as CMS. The company was operating there before it was acquired by private equity. In North Dakota, CMS owns three of the state’s four methadone clinics. In Arizona, CMS owns the Sierra Vista clinic where Titus gets her methadone. Amber Titus, 38, leaves her appointment at Community Medical Services’ methadone clinic in Sierra Vista, Ariz., on Sept. 18. Daniela Dawson, CC BY-ND In 2018, a prospective investor advised shutting down CMS’ Montana and North Dakota clinics as unprofitable. Nick Stavros, CEO of CMS, opted to partner with a different private equity firm to keep the clinics open. Before private equity investment, CMS had 14 clinics in four states. It now has 79 clinics in 14 states, according to Stavros. The total includes five clinics in prisons and three mobile units. Unlike the typical private equity investment strategy of acquisitions, a majority of the company’s recent growth – 49 clinics – has come from new sites, he said. No expansion has taken place in Montana. Building a new clinic costs about $2.5 million, more than many rural areas can support, Stavros said. Proponents of private equity ownership argue it can help fill gaps left by inadequate public funding for addiction treatment. The strongest evidence in their favor: One study found clinics became significantly more likely to accept Medicare and Medicaid after acquisition, likely because large chains can afford administrative infrastructure that small, independent clinics cannot. That’s a real benefit worth acknowledging. But look past insurance acceptance and ask whether more people are actually getting – and staying on – treatment, and the picture darkens. For buprenorphine, a related medication that can be prescribed more broadly than methadone, one study found patient volume at private equity-acquired facilities rose about 22% after acquisition. Similar data for methadone was not available. But the same study found the share of patients who stayed continuously on buprenorphine for 180 days – the national quality benchmark – fell by nearly 8 percentage points. Early discontinuation is one of the strongest predictors of relapse and overdose. A proposal to expand methadone access These findings matter beyond academic journals, because they are at the heart of an active policy debate. Congress is weighing the Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act 2.0, which would let regular doctors prescribe methadone and let pharmacies dispense it, breaking the decades-old rule that methadone can be dispensed only at opioid treatment programs. The Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act was introduced in 2023. After facing opposition, it did not reach a House or Senate vote before the end of the congressional term. Lawmakers later reintroduced the bill with changes as Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act 2.0, which is currently in consideration by the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees. The committees have not yet scheduled the next step, a markup of the bill, and the current congressional term ends in January 2027. In an email, U.S. Rep. Donald Norcross, D-N.J., one of the bill’s sponsors, recalled a snowstorm years earlier when he noticed a single track of footprints crossing an otherwise empty street to a methadone clinic. “I realized that no matter what else is happening in the world,” Norcross said, “some of our neighbors’ lives literally revolve around getting to that building every single day.” Methadone for opioid use disorder is typically taken orally, most often as a liquid. Daniela Dawson, CC BY-ND The bill has widespread support from patient advocacy organizations and medical societies. At the same time, a STAT investigation found that the main opposition to the legislation comes from the American Association for the Treatment of Opioid Dependence, AATOD, a major trade group representing methadone clinics. This coalition argues that expanded prescribing and pharmacy dispensing of methadone would increase diversion and overdose risk. The evidence so far does not support that claim. Moreover, firms that control large shares of their local markets may have a financial incentive to keep new competitors, including doctors and pharmacies, out. Mark Parrino, AATOD’s president, told The Conversation the trade group opposes the bill for two reasons. First, the bill would let the Health and Human Services secretary determine which additional practitioners are qualified to prescribe methadone for opioid use disorder. Second, it would allow methadone to be dispensed in dispersible tablet as well as liquid form. Tablets “were definitely” involved in a rise in methadone-related deaths that began around 1999, Parrino said. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and a Food and Drug Administration advisory tied those deaths to methadone prescribed for pain, not addiction treatment. Stavros, who is AATOD’s Arizona representative, said he did not see the bill as a threat to CMS’ business model, but he cited concerns that removing all regulation too quickly could allow a few bad providers to drive up methadone overdoses and increase stigma against the drug. “We need to find ways to increase access,” he said. “If somebody would come up with … a slow, gradual transition that led to pharmacy prescribing,” Stavros said he would support it. Dr. Melody Glenn, associate professor of addiction and emergency medicine at the University of Arizona, previously worked at a methadone clinic in Tucson and supports MOTAA 2.0, though she said the legislation should go further. “It’s time to remove the regulatory barriers to these lifesaving medications,” Glenn told The Conversation in an email. The bill would allow doctors specializing in addiction medicine, like her, to prescribe methadone. Glenn said it’s frustrating that such an effective treatment for opioid use disorder exists, yet many people who could benefit never receive it. “They don’t have to die,” she said. Bringing private equity deals into view Two other policy responses are gaining traction. The first is ownership transparency. Regulators, researchers and patients cannot scrutinize what they cannot see, yet private equity is exempt from the disclosure rules that apply to publicly traded companies. Indiana, California and Maine have enacted or proposed reform to disclose private equity and management company ownership as a condition of being able to bill Medicare or Medicaid. Vermont passed similar legislation this year, on which I was invited to provide expert testimony. The second is lowering the reporting threshold for acquiring a healthcare company to make them more visible to agencies enforcing U.S. antitrust laws, which are intended to promote competition and prevent monopolies. The U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission consider ownership of 30% or more of a local market for a product or service a red flag for anticompetitive behavior. Yet, as my research shows, private equity chains typically control at least 67% of a local methadone market within two years of their first clinic purchase in a county. The reason most never trigger the federal reporting requirement is because these acquisitions happen through a series of smaller, piecemeal deals rather than one large merger. The reporting requirement applies only to deals worth more than about $134 million. Some states have introduced proposals to lower thresholds to around $10 million specifically for healthcare deals, so the vast majority become visible to enforcement agencies before they close. Structural barriers to getting treatment The U.S. is experiencing an ongoing and severe opioid crisis. In 2023, approximately 80% of the more than 100,000 drug overdose deaths involved an opioid. b6cda9ccbb3e6f68: State surveillance and policing of online expression have a long history in the country
Originally published on Global Voices
Photo by cottonbro studio. Used under a Pexels License.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Bangladesh is revising its cyber law to tackle AI-generated images, and the draft has triggered a furious debate over how much the state should police speech online. The ICT Division published the draft Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act for public comment in mid-September. It is now with a five-member cabinet committee led by Posts, Telecommunications and ICT Minister Faqir Mahbub Anam. In a discussion reported on October 19, media figures, legal analysts, and civil society representatives called for the most contested clauses to be removed.

The push follows a campaign season crowded with synthetic media. Global Voices previously reported on a study that identified 72 AI-manipulated items that gained traction between December 2025 and the February 12, 2026 election. Synthetic images of political figures were the most common tactic, alongside doctored news-channel graphics. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), which went on to win, was the most frequent target, with 47 cases.

State surveillance and policing of online expression have a long history. Section 57 of the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Act of 2006 punished online content seen as defamatory, hurtful to religious sentiment, or damaging to the state’s image. A 2013 amendment toughened it, with sentences of up to 14 years. Journalists and ordinary social media users were among those charged under it. After years of protest, the government promised to scrap Section 57. Yet when the Digital Security Act (DSA) was signed into law in October 2018, the same offenses reappeared in sections 25, 28, 29 and 31. By 2023, the law minister had told parliament that 7,001 cases had been filed under it. The writer Mushtaq Ahmed died in custody in 2021 after ten months in jail under the DSA, which led to protests at home and abroad.

The Awami League government replaced the DSA with the Cyber Security Act in 2023, but Amnesty International said it repackaged almost all of the DSA’s repressive features. After the July 2024 uprising, the interim government scrapped nine sections through a new Cyber Security Ordinance in 2025. Rights groups say hundreds of cases from earlier years are still pending.
Fakes in the election and beyond

Women in politics faced a particular kind of attack. A Daily Star analysis of AI content before the vote found that pro-Awami League pages targeted female leaders of the National Citizen Party (NCP) with fabricated images that hinted at moral and sexual impropriety. After the election, a Prothom Alo fact-check found AI-generated images and invented statements aimed at nominees for reserved women's seats. Tanvir Mahatab Abir of Rumor Scanner told the paper that visible women, especially in politics, are frequent targets of disinformation.

Not all of it is political. Data from the Daily Star shows that Facebook pages used deepfake videos of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and his family, including his daughter Zaima Rahman, to promote fake “Family Card” offers in exchange for likes and follows. Among 52 posts analyzed, 13 featured Zaima. One page administrator told the fact-checking outlet Dismislab that the aim was to gain followers quickly and sell the pages. In such cases, for many creators of synthetic content, monetization metrics on social platforms often serve as a primary driver alongside political motives.
A case that left no remedy

For ordinary women, the damage can last much longer. Farzana Sithi, a student activist known for her role in the historic student-led uprising in 2024, was targeted by a fake Facebook profile that Dismislab investigated in March 2025. Of 166 videos and reels posted between December 13, 2024, and March 17, 2025, 133 were AI-generated deepfakes. They placed her face on videos of two Indian content creators. The five most-viewed clips drew more than 4.1 million views, and the account was monetized through Facebook's Stars feature.

“These videos are an attempt to tarnish my character,” Sithi told Dismislab, adding that she was bullied and shamed as a result. She reported the profile to Facebook several times. IT experts she approached privately asked for USD 100 to USD 150 to remove the fake accounts and videos, which she said she could not afford. At the time of Dismislab’s report, the profile was still active. Comments under the reels included rape threats.
What the law covers, and what the draft would change

Legal experts point out that the existing legislative framework has struggled to keep pace with rapid advancements in synthetic media. The Cyber Protection Act was enacted on 10 April 2026 and amended on 30 June. Its Section 25 already covers blackmail, sexual harassment, revenge porn, child sexual abuse material, sextortion and the distribution of AI-generated or manipulated content.

According to the minister, these offenses carry up to two years in prison, or up to five if the victim is a woman or under 18. The law targets AI mainly when it is used to commit existing crimes. It does not set out a dedicated framework for synthetic media or political deepfakes.

The draft would change that. It adds defamation, humiliation and bullying to Section 25 and names AI-generated content explicitly. A prior investigation by Prothom Alo revealed that the maximum penalty would rise to five years in prison and a BDT 2 million fine (roughly USD 16,131), and to ten years and Tk 4 million if the target is a woman or a person under 18. A new Section 26A would punish publishing or spreading a “rumor” or “disinformation” with up to ten years in prison, a fine of BDT 4 million (roughly USD 32,262), or both. The draft defines a rumor as unverified information that causes or risks causing confusion, panic or social instability.

The government presents the changes as a response to harm already being done. Introducing an earlier amendment in June, the ICT minister said it would require platforms such as Meta to remove disputed content within a set time. Officials told Prothom Alo that the tougher penalties are meant to curb fake videos, audio and images made with AI.
Free speech concerns

Critics say the draft goes well beyond that aim. Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) warned that terms such as “rumor” and “demeaning” are defined loosely enough to allow selective enforcement. A joint statement by rights groups said the draft mirrors the repealed Digital Security Act. The Committee to Protect Journalists has objected to the prospect of journalists facing criminal liability for reporting officials consider unverified. An Asia Times analysis noted that because defamation sits inside Section 25, the heavier penalty for offenses against women would apply to it as well, and not only to sexual abuse.
Numbers, gaps and local responses

What the law would address is substantial. A report by Dhaka Tribune said police's Cyber Support for Women unit had been approached by 60,808 women by September 2024, and cited a 2024 Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics–UNFPA survey in which nearly 89 percent of women social media users reported online violence at least once. Officials say the real number is likely higher because of underreporting. The published figures do not separate cases involving AI.

Researchers describe a similar pattern across the region. A study in the Journal of Online Trust and Safety drew on three workshops with 49 journalists, lawyers, fact-checkers and advocates in Sri Lanka, India and Bangladesh. It found that women are disproportionately targeted, that platform moderation often fails in South Asian languages, and that victims struggle to reach institutional help. Sithi's (a student activist known for her role in the historic student-led uprising in 2024) experience, where the cost of private help was out of reach, fits that last finding.

Digital skills are an added concern. The Asian Development Bank reports that functional digital literacy in Bangladesh stands at 49 percent and that rural users are 29 percent less likely than urban users to use mobile internet. Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics data released in April show that 56.6 percent of men use the internet, against 50.2 percent of women. Advocates argue that people with fewer digital skills may find it harder to spot manipulated media or seek redress. These surveys, however, do not measure exposure to deepfakes directly.

Outside the government, fact-checkers are trying to keep pace. FactFest 2026, held on 27–28 September, brought together around 100 fact-checkers, journalists and researchers, according to an organizer. Its 13 sessions covered AI and gendered disinformation, among other topics. In the closing roundtable, speakers said Bangladeshi fact-checkers face shrinking funding and weak coordination with mainstream newsrooms.

The cabinet committee has yet to finalize the draft, which would then go to Parliament. Constitution Watchdog, a civil society group, has urged the government to withdraw the draft in its present form and reopen public consultation for at least 30 days. It also acknowledged the government's stated aim of protecting women and children from online abuse and responding to deepfakes. Whether a narrower law can do that without the speech provisions now under attack is the question facing lawmakers.
Written by Masudul Zarif

9e57b3c7cb0d7eb2: The crack of a bat accompanied by a roar from the crowd can capture a baseball fan’s attention, even if they miss seeing the home run. Humans may be visual creatures, but we also perceive the world around us by listening to it.  To improve artificial perception, MIT Professor Paris Smaragdis SM ’97, PhD ’01 seeks to make machines that can hear and understand sound even better than humans. A machine with super-human hearing could rapidly pinpoint the location of a traffic accident by listening for squealing tires and crunching metal, or identify when an industrial drill might break while it is boring through dense bedrock to dig a geothermal well. “I like to say that I do the same thing the computer vision folks do, but instead I do it for hearing,” says Smaragdis, a professor in the Music and Theatre Arts program of the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. His research group explores areas like machine learning for sound source separation, smart devices that can augment the audio surroundings of humans, and better tools to help people understand, manipulate, analyze, and create music. “Having had a musical background, I’ve been interested in examining these ideas. What does it take to make machines understand sound? There is a huge domain of applications for machines that can listen,” says Smaragdis, who joined MIT in 2025 and is also part of the Music Technology program and a member of the Research Laboratory of Electronics. A musical prelude Smaragdis, who grew up in Greece, began playing classical guitar at a young age. He enjoyed playing traditional pieces but reached a turning point in his musical journey when his father brought home a small synthesizer. “That little synthesizer had a function that allowed you to make your own sounds, and I became completely captivated by the possibilities,” he says. Synthesizers were taking a more prominent place in pop music during the 1980s, adding to his fascination with the technology. As he advanced through school, Smaragdis wanted to study music made with synthesizers. But this was not an educational path offered by the more traditional European conservatories at the time. Instead, he enrolled at Berklee College of Music in Boston, into a program where he could explore the use of computers and synthesizers to shape and manipulate sound. “With computers and synthesizers, I could make new sounds that have never been heard before,” he says. At the same time, Smaragdis became immersed in jazz fusion. He declared bass as his major at Berklee since it would allow him more opportunities to play with jazz ensembles. “I found the bass to be sonically more interesting than the guitar. It was a more unexplored domain, and I’ve always gravitated toward unexplored domains,” he says. That interest in the unexplored carried over into his coursework. He and mentor Richard Boulanger, a professor of electronic production and design, created new tools to help people use computers to write, produce, and enhance music.  Through his studies at Berklee, Smaragdis embarked on a collaborative project with Professor Barry Vercoe (who passed away in 2025) at the MIT Media Lab to create software synthesizers for music creation. Building on that project, Smaragdis pursued graduate studies in Vercoe’s group, where he completed his master’s degree and PhD, followed by a postdoc. “In the Media Lab, I got exposed more to the computer part of computer music. That’s where my attention shifted a bit. Now I really wanted to make computers that could understand sound,” he says. Tuning in to unexplored domains At that time, many students in the Media Lab were using signal processing techniques to help machines handle sound. Smaragdis chose a less explored approach — machine learning — to separate himself from the pack. He found that training machine-learning models to understand sound offered advantages that couldn’t be attained with traditional signal processing techniques. “Over time, it became really clear to me that we need to teach computers how to listen. We can’t just tell them how to listen. If anything, we don’t even know how we humans listen,” he says. “We don’t have a vocabulary to explain what it means to listen, or how to tell the difference between a cat’s meow and the sound of a violin.” After finishing his postdoc, Smaragdis began a career at Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs, where he worked on artificial intelligence systems that could scan video soundtracks and understand what is happening on screen.  “What if you record an entire soccer game, but you only want to watch the highlights? In computer vision, it is very difficult to identify what a highlight is. But on the other hand, if you only listen to the sounds, then when the crowd goes crazy you would know that something interesting is happening,” he says. That system was eventually incorporated into electronic devices, including a personal video recording system Mitsubishi was developing at the time, and into traffic monitoring systems and cell phones. Smaragdis later joined Adobe, where he created the audio research team that built user-friendly tools to help artists, musicians, and producers manipulate sound without needing a lot of expertise. “As we did that work, I kept coming up with deeper technical problems that needed to be resolved. I jumped into academia to address that itch,” he says. Smaragdis joined the faculty at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where he and his group incorporated the latest machine-learning techniques into audio-processing systems. One of the technologies they developed utilized neural networks for separating individual sounds from audio mixtures. That project caught the attention of the team working on the 2021 documentary mini-series “The Beatles: Get Back.” The production team enlisted Smaragdis to help clean up some archival Beatles recordings. “That was a very different way of audio processing than what I was doing in academia. Now, I had to do something that sounded good but didn’t necessarily have to look good on paper. We didn’t have a formula we could optimize,” he says. Every recording involved different challenges. For instance, in one clip John Lennon was playing music while Paul McCartney was horsing around, reading headlines from newspapers and making fun of George Harrison. “We were trying to come up with a technological solution that could help us do everything, as opposed to addressing each problem on its own,” he says. His contributions helped the team win an Emmy Award for sound editing for a nonfiction or reality program, in 2022. A concerted effort After 15 years at the University of Illinois, Smaragdis decided to join the faculty at MIT to tackle the thorny, interdisciplinary problems that were emerging in the field.  His group now focuses on two main areas. For one, they develop systems that make computers more useful tools for musicians.  One project in this area is enabling machines to understand how to listen to music, so they can provide constructive feedback to musicians. “We want to enhance the toolbox a musician has. We don’t want to use computers to replace musicians,” he says. On the other side, his group focuses on the fundamental tools scientists and artists alike can use to process, analyze, and manipulate audio. For instance, his team has recently been exploring algorithms that allow sophisticated signal processing where traditional frames of reference, such as sampling rates, frame sizes, or context-windows, are not fixed — or even defined.  That implies different computational structures that are yet unexplored, despite their potential for more efficient processing, Smaragdis says. “That requires rethinking a lot of the basics, but once you have that ability, you can start getting much more flexible and more powerful systems,” he adds. They also explore ways to incorporate the latest techniques, like large language models, into speech recognition and audio enhancement. “AI is an immensely powerful tool, but I don’t think we have found the ideal way to use it for sound and music yet,” he says. He also enjoys mentoring students and helping them materialize their visions for research projects. Since few of his students have experience using computation in sound, he emphasizes hands-on lessons so they see and hear how to transform equations into something tangible. Smaragdis still feels a thrill from making music, whether with a computer or a more traditional instrument. Off campus, he tries to play jazz bass whenever he can find the time, and enjoys exploring the rich musical community of Boston with his wife and 15-year-old son. Outside the musical realm, he plays and coaches underwater hockey — a sport where players wear diving masks and use sticks to push a heavy puck across the bottom of a pool toward their opponent’s goal. He coached the underwater hockey team at the University of Illinois, and is hoping to revive the MIT underwater hockey club soon and start hosting tournaments on campus. While underwater hockey may be a lesser-known sport, it fits with Smaragdis’ lifelong interest in pursuing the underexplored. “I’ve always like doing things that were different from what everyone else was doing. If you can create a new sound that no one has heard before, what does that mean about your ability to create new things? I still find these questions completely fascinating,” he says.

A school should be a place where children feel safe, friendships flourish, differences are respected, and every child knows that someone cares.
